utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bulatovic. We will continue in a moment with your examination by Mr. Fila. Please bear in mind throughout today that the solemn declaration to speak the truth, which you gave at the beginning of your evidence, continues to apply throughout. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I hope you had a pleasant evening last night. We will now move on to a different topic and that is Rambouillet. Did the federal government play any role in the negotiations in Rambouillet in Paris?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The federal government's role was to form the political platform for those negotiations. The standpoints were practically the same as those adopted on the 5th of October by the Federal Assembly. We spoke about those yesterday. That was the unified political position of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did the government send any deputy prime ministers to the delegation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the negotiating team of the Republic of Serbia, that was the level at which the negotiations were held and decisions made, were Nikola Sainovic, the deputy prime minister, as the person tasked by the federal government to be in charge of foreign relations; and also Mr. Kutlesic who was a legal expert and he was the personal envoy of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Slobodan Milosevic, within the delegation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You certainly know what was asked of our delegation in Rambouillet, as regards accepting foreign troops in order to implement the agreement. What was the standpoint of our country and the federal government in this respect?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I did not attend the negotiations myself, I cannot talk about the course they took. I can only talk about the political repercussions felt in the federal government and the FRY. Unfortunately, the general view was that these were not really negotiations. They were negotiations without negotiations. The main issue was implementing the ten principles of the Contact Group which were the basis for the negotiations. For our country, in terms of politics, the first nine principles were quite acceptable. We had problems with the tenth principle. If I remember correctly, it said "foreign presence" in the implementation of the agreement. We did not know whether "foreign presence" implied a military component or not. That's why, in the cabinet, we had a lively discussion about whether it was possible to accept this tenth principle if it meant a military presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please now look at document 2D221, tab 12. As you see this is a document of the federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And it represents the standpoint of the ministry. Please tell us who this document was addressed to and what it means.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sent to the federal prime minister and the cabinet by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, asking that the position of the foreign ministry be discussed and that if they are adopted they should become the standpoints of the federal government. This is the diplomatic response of our ministry to the military annex offered to the negotiators in Rambouillet. There is a suggestion here that our diplomacy holds the standpoint that the FRY, starting from its constitution and constitutional obligations, should not accept the possibility of a foreign military presence. Just allow me to finish, please. This is completely identical to the standpoint the Ministry of Foreign Affairs adopted when the verification mission of the OSCE was established in Kosovo and Metohija. A compromise had been found, I wish to remind Their Honours, in that it was unarmed observers with military experience who made up that mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And was this standpoint adopted?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was adopted in the form in which we see it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And there is a communique to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now please look at document 2D294, tab 13.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm very nostalgic when I see this document. It was my duty as the country whose prime minister I was without any warning was attacked with cruise missiles; and at that point in time, when a state of war was declared, we did what we had to do under the constitution and our laws, although we did not know who had attacked the country, why, or with what consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, please look at tab 14, document 2D299. First, tell us what sort of document this is, and please take a look at page 2 especially.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document, in its bureaucratic form, is not a pure document, but it is a communique issued by the federal cabinet addressed to the world as an appeal to the world for humanitarian assistance. It's a response to the situation which had arisen in the FRY which had been attacked by NATO. It was subject to aggression. The fact that there is no tidy heading shows that the government was operating under impossible conditions, but I can confirm the authenticity of this text. I especially wish to point out that the government appealed to all the refugees. The greatest number of refugees were Albanians, so this was addressed primarily to them. This was not done as a kind of political marketing. It was actually an expression of the sincere commitment of the federal government to have people stay on their hearths and homes and for us to order a joint life together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the date of this appeal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was early October -- excuse me, or rather, early April 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, look at document 2D301, tab 15. Please look at the paragraph before the last on the first page and tell us what government -- what kind of document this is and what it means.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The form is a communique from a session of the federal cabinet. This was the usual way in which the federal cabinet communicated with the public and informed it of its political standpoints and its decisions. The paragraph you are drawing attention to says: "The federal government has repeated its appeal that they should not leave there and our state and that they can themselves raise their voice against the frenzy of the NATO killers. By ending the aggression, the conditions will be created for an all-encompassing political solution in Kosovo and Metohija." Both in its grammar and wording, this appeal is addressed to all ethnic Albanians in Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. When was the document issued?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 4th of April. I recognise here the interventions I made in my own hand because, at that time, in the building of the federal cabinet which was announced to be a target of the air-strikes, I had said that no clerks or civil servants were to be present. I was there myself with only a few people.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know anything about Sainovic's activities after the beginning of the war in connection with Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His most important activity, of which we all expected results, was to establish political contacts and dialogue with Mr. Ibrahim Rugova. Mr. Ibrahim Rugova was a man we disagreed with. As far as I can recall in 1991, at an illegal referendum and elections, he was declared president of Kosovo, but nobody in the world accepted this or recognised it. However, he was a man who had undisputed -- an undisputed standing among the Kosovo Albanians, and it was our commitment in our desire to establish a dialogue with the Albanians to do so through their leader, Mr. Ibrahim Rugova.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what month was this in the spring of 1990 [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a period where there was a goal that we wanted to achieve. We were persistent in wanting to establish a dialogue. And could you remind me, I know there must be some documents, but I can't remember the date really.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is an error in the transcript. It says in the spring of 1990. I said in the spring of 1999. Can that be corrected, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now please look at tab 16. The document is 2D365.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document now refreshes my memory. I now remember precisely. When the president of Yugoslavia, Slobodan Milosevic, and Dr. Ibrahim Rugova met on the 1st of April, 1999, this footage was broadcast on the national television service in Serbia and gave rise to polemics. Many people thought that Ibrahim Rugova had long been dead, and they -- there was a lot of discussion about whether the footage was real or not, but fortunately they were wrong. The political dialogue was supposed to start, and I can see that there is a joint communique here which was issued after Nikola Sainovic's meeting with Dr. Ibrahim Rugova on the 5th of April, 1999, where they agreed, and this was a significant step forward in resolving the political situation in Kosovo and Metohija to continue working jointly on the political process, in order to solve the issue of Kosovo and to work together to bring back refugees and displaced citizens to their homes. My understanding is that in this way Dr. Ibrahim Rugova joined the repeated appeals of the federal government, that refugees and displaced persons should return to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is this the activity of Nikola Sainovic you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And it started before that, of course, in March and continued in April?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To achieve such a major goal, to have people of such different political affiliations meet, people of such different background, a lot of effort and time is needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, please look at document 1D36, tab 17. This is a communique. Tell us what sort of communique this is.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something that was issued on the same day or the next day. It's a joint statement of the federal government and the Government of the Republic of Serbia. It was the custom, politically, that when one wanted to attach special weight to a certain standpoint, the greatest number possible of state organs and institutions should stand behind it. What happened here was that two governments agreed on a text and issued a joint statement. In the first sentence, in the preamble, it says: "The federal government of the FRY and the Government of the Republic of Serbia at their separate sessions adopted the following joint statement." I won't go on reading, but the principles enshrined here are a continuation of the same policy. But the fact that a joint statement was issued shows that both governments, with their constitutional and legal competencies, were aspiring to absolutely the same goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And that was?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To stabilise the political situation, the return of refugees, the start of a political dialogue, and everything that would lead to a permanent stabilisation of the situation in Kosovo and Metohija. In paragraph 3 or point 3, it says: "Together with representatives of Albanians represented by Dr. Rugova, a programme of return of refugees should be prepared with the appropriate participation and assistance of the UNHCR and the International Committee of the Red Cross." So, again, with the verification and presence of unchallenged international institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, please look at document 2D303, tab 18.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document, I can confirm its authenticity, and it is a statement from the meeting of the federal government, although there is no stamp or signature. I remember it quite well. It was dated the 8th of April, 1999. Only a few days after the federal and republican governments had informed the world public, the international public, about the possibility of the start of a real dialogue with Dr. Ibrahim Rugova and the solving of the most serious issue in Kosovo and Metohija, and that was the return of refugees, the most severe NATO air-strikes against civilian targets on Kosovo and Metohija occurred. In those days - and this was completely unexpected - huge amounts of explosives were dropped on the civilian part of Pristina, numerous buildings were destroyed, and the message was more than clear. Evidently, the stabilisation and dialogue that had started here caused this reaction. Unfortunately, this was very clear. This was the beginning of the end of the dialogue which had barely started.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So your conclusion was that NATO met this possibility with great enthusiasm, right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We just put two and two together in this case, and the result was very sad. We believed it wasn't possible for this sort of military power to be dispatched at a moment like that, because there was at least some hope of dialogue emanating at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did Sainovic do any other jobs in relation to Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, this was his only job in Kosovo and Metohija. Unfortunately, the project was an important one, yet unsuccessful. After that, Sainovic returned to Belgrade and went back to his work with the government and the wartime conditions. However, his job and the job of the rest of us, who were members, of the government meant nothing more than regulating the circumstances that prevailed among the civilians which required an enormous amount of effort. Chemical factories in Serbia were attacked 23 times, for example, if only one of those shells had hit its target we would have had an environmental disaster --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he answered the question, and now he's going on to make some kind of a speech. The question was did he do any other jobs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, if you want to deal with an additional matter, then please pose another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, Serbia's Minister of Energy was heard before the court, Mr. Cosic. He said Mr. Sainovic was involved in trying to avert possible disasters resulting from the NATO air-strikes targeting chemical factories. We would have all been killed, just wiped out, all of us, all together --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the speakers not overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, two matters arise here. First of all, you're not observing a break between the question and the answer, and you're causing great difficulty for the interpreters; and, secondly, that's one of the best examples of a leading question we've had in the case yet. The answer is going to be of little value, in view of the fact that you've given the witness the answer. So it might have been better to give him an open question, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was Mr. Sainovic's job during the war following his return from Kosovo while he was a member of your cabinet?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was precisely what I was trying to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, just a second. The objection was perfectly well-stated by Mr. Hannis because the question related to whether he had done anything else in relation to Kosovo, and you went on to deal with issues unrelated directly to Kosovo. That's why the objection was taken. So it's wrong of you to criticise the interruption that took place here, and the correct way to deal with this is to confine the answers to the specific questions that are asked. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know if there were any air-strikes targeting chemical factories?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, there were 23 such attacks. There were attacks on schools, on the insane asylums. There was systematic killing of civilians of our country --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object again. He answered the question, and now he's going on to make a speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question related to the targeting of chemical factories, Mr. Bulatovic. Now, please confine your answers to what you're asked. It will not enhance your evidence if we form the impression that you've come here to stage a political platform, which on more than one occasion has happened in this Tribunal. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did Mr. Sainovic have any tasks within your cabinet such as to deal with the consequences of NATO air-strikes in relation to chemical factories, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was something done by Nikola Sainovic and also by all the other ministers in the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was Mr. Sainovic during the war in any way involved in commanding the defence forces in Kosovo and Metohija be the army or police?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Based on all of my information, both the military and the police in Kosovo and Metohija acted perfectly in compliance with their constitutional and legal powers. The federal cabinet had no power in terms of exercising command over any unit of the MUP or the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That Sainovic should interfere with the command without you knowing?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would have been impossible for him to go behind my back and do anything like that. Secondly, I knew the police general and the army generals, I know they would have had no such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Have you ever heard a term "Joint Command"?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Joint Command" or --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: "Joint Command," have you heard that term, have you ever heard it used?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First time I heard this term was when the indictment was published in this case and the indictment against Milosevic. This term never existed in our reality or in our constitutional system for that matter. There was joint activity. The left hand must know what the right hand is doing, but this term "Joint Command" is something I'm entirely unfamiliar with and I would say no such thing existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you aware of a joint enterprise that arose in 1998 and continued to exist in 1998 and 1999, its objective being to expel Albanians from Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I am unaware of any such plan. I've never heard of it. The only reference I did here were the references in the two indictments of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said something about Dayton, you talked about ethnic groups, and so on and so forth. What was the principle formulated by Dayton in terms of ethnic minorities?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me remind the honourable Chamber, this was in October and November 1995, the Dayton conference; whereas, the war in the former Yugoslavia had broken out early in June 1991. Four years had elapsed. There had been many negotiations in Geneva, in Brussels, and this is what it took to try to implement several different peace plans which eventually led to the Dayton conference which was successful. The main principle formulated there was equal rights for all ethnic groups. This was eventually recognised at the Dayton conference, and this applied to the Muslims, Bosniaks, Croats, and Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was the plan that eventually brought peace, and it was eventually implemented. This is the key principle in the Balkans to deal with ethnic strife, with ethnic issues, equal rights for everyone. You can't have peace if you know in advance who the bad guys are and who the good guys are, thereby creating a vicious circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you think there would have been any problems trying to apply that sort of principle in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the only principle that I think we ever applied in our many dealings with Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was the political position espoused by Nikola Sainovic in relation to these political principles and in relation to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sainovic was a member of the Socialist Party of Serbia. There were many, many people in that party who came from all sorts of ethnic groups. This wasn't a purely Serbian party or a purely socialist party. I think this speaks for itself, and it shows you what his position was. Throughout my work with Sainovic, I realised that he earnestly believed in the possibility and need for dialogue, that an agreement had to be reached by everyone, and that this would then lead to a peaceful continuation of our lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would like to move on to something different now, Mr. Sainovic [as interpreted]. This is a new subject for me, and it's also the last subject that I would like to deal with. I'm talking about the Supreme Defence Council. You, as federal prime minister, attended meetings of the Supreme Defence Council, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the constitution of the FRY, the Supreme Defence Council was a body comprising the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. It also included the presidents of all of the republics. There was a -- there were rules of procedure in place, and this is how the meetings and the work were organised. I know this not only based on theory but also because I was actively involved in the work of the council between February 1993 and 1998 as the president of Montenegro. Who was involved? The federal prime minister who was to all practical intents in charge of logistics, so to speak. The defence minister was involved as well; and sometimes based on a special invitation, a third person could be involved; for example, the minister of foreign affairs or anyone else from the military, for example. They would take part in the work of the council, and the same thing applied to the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, who was also actively involved in the work of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But the only those three had the right to vote and take decisions, right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The members of the Supreme Defence Council had the right to vote. The rest of us were just attached to this body, and we tried to help them with their decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What if the federal prime minister was busy doing something else, could he have dispatched one of his assistants to stand in for him at one of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, this only happened once. There is no matter more urgent, more pressing than attending meetings like these; however, I believe there were personal reasons, private reasons, at stake here. So sometime in late December 1998, I appointed deputy prime minister, Mr. Sainovic, to stand in for me at one of these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why him of all people?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This meeting was about Kosovo and Metohija. They were talking about Kosovo and Metohija, and that is precisely what he was involved with, so he seemed like the most logical choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What is the mechanism for decision-making in the Supreme Defence Council? What exactly do they do and are their decisions publicly announced?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can discuss the two different periods. The first period, when I was the member of the Supreme Defence Council, yes, of course, we took decisions about everything that happened to be on our agenda; otherwise, it would have been totally meaningless, and it would have amounted to no more than a private discussion club. But we took decisions in accordance with proposals issuing from the relevant bodies in each of the cases. None of us were experts in military matters, and I think this applies throughout the world whenever you see a country that is based on the democratic principles. The Supreme Defence Council must pick one of the options open to it, option A and option B, and they must back the chosen option with their reputations, with their authority. And this included some people who worked in the defence ministry and the Army of Yugoslavia. But the strategic level of these decisions was enormous, and this is the sort of decision that must be taken by the president of the republic and by the president of all the other republics that the Supreme Defence Council comprised. When push comes to shove, you need someone who will say: We pick option A as opposed to option B.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on a moment. The interpreter did not hear that question. Could we have it repeated, please, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I asked you about the nature of those decisions.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were strategic decisions at the upper-most level. There is no one in the country that can possibly adopt a decision more important than this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said they were strategic decisions, right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I also asked you whether these decisions were published in the Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was for a while the army Official Gazette, and some of the decisions were published. Indirectly, decisions on the appointment of generals are normally published in the form of an ordinance, but I really can't answer your question very specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Talking about the use of the units of the Army of Yugoslavia, how did that work?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, take this example: The Chief of the General Staff --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Rather, can you please go to P1574, which is tab 19.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please go to page 3 of that document, and can you please explain what I've just asked you based on that example.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are minutes of a Supreme Defence Council meeting held on the 9th of June, 1998. We see the results of that meeting on page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could I stop you so that I can clarify one measure of confusion at the moment. You divided the answer, at least you indicated that you would divide the answer into two periods: The first period would be when you were, yourself, a member, a voting member of the Supreme Defence Council; and the second period, no doubt, is when you attended as the federal prime minister. I thought that what you were describing so far was the period when you were a voting member, but does your answer that you've given up to now cover both the period when you were president of Montenegro and the period when you were the federal prime minister?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The difference is about my familiarity with details as to how the Supreme Defence Council actually worked. While I was a member myself, I was driven by a powerful motive to pay close attention to each and every detail, including --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but let me stop you again now. So when you say that the members of the Supreme Defence Council made strategic decisions at the upper-most level, that applies both to the period when you were president of Montenegro and the period when you were federal prime minister; is that correct? I need to hear an answer. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think the document that Mr. Fila has just brought up will shed light on this dilemma, but, yes, you are quite right my statement goes to both of these periods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the reason - sorry, Mr. Fila - the reason I interrupted at that stage was because the document you have just referred to relates to the period when the witness was no longer president of Montenegro but was federal prime minister and we had moved ahead, and I'm sorry to have interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please don't apologise for interrupting. I believe that it's only useful when you interrupt and even when Mr. Hannis interrupts.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You've had a look at this, and on page -- well, actually please look at page 3 and explain this to us. What can be derived on the basis of this document?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a debate that went on for hours. The basis for this discussion was to be very accurate in terms of time, dates, and facts, and that was contained in the introductory remarks of the Chief of General Staff. All of these military papers end with a proposal of concrete measures and activities that are derived from the constitutional and legal position of the army; therefore, the decision under number 1 means the following: The remarks of the Chief of General Staff are accepted, that is to say, General Perisic's remarks. That means that when the Supreme Defence Council rules in this way, that the statement made by the Chief of General Staff are accepted, that means that the conclusions proposed by the Chief of General Staff hereby turn into decisions of the Supreme Defence Council. The second conclusion is not an indefinite one. If terrorist activities escalate, the army will intervene appropriately. This conclusion is supposed to be established in relation to what the Chief of General Staff said. He had already portrayed the level of terrorist activity and the reaction of the Army of Yugoslavia. So the strategic decision is that if there is an increase of that which we already know of, the other will be increased as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And further on?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Third, the Army of Yugoslavia will be prepared for intervening if there is any foreign intervention against the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Yugoslavia. After all, that is the basic postulate for any army of the world, the Army of Yugoslavia included.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So in your opinion, in your opinion, the Supreme Defence Council accepted the position of General Perisic and made a decision to act in this way in case what General Perisic said actually took place?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a further implementation of what General Perisic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So the military is used in two cases: If there is an escalation of terrorism or an attack from the outside; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That decision comes into force automatically.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Should such a decision be published in the Official Gazette, and does that happen anywhere in the world?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time we did not have a secret Official Gazette or a military Official Gazette, so we could not have published that. As far as I know, no one in the world would have published any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: On the basis of this decision of the Supreme Defence Council, as you have put it, what did the federal government do when you were federal prime minister, and also the minister who was in your cabinet, did you take any measures? Did the government take any measures on the basis of what was otherwise in its jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It is the task of the government to make it possible for a government -- for a state to function normally but for all the segments for which it is in charge. And we had a Ministry of Defence; therefore, it conducts preparations for defending the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just a second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I consult with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since my learned friend has no suggestions, I will conclude as far as my questions are concerned, and I would like to remind the Chamber of the following, that I have spent two hours and 30 minutes including your interventions and including Mr. Hannis's interventions. I have, thereby, left more than four hours for cross-examination. I'm saying this because Mr. Bulatovic has to be in Belgrade tomorrow for urgent family reasons. The Trial Chamber ruled that the Prosecution should have time equal to mine, and the rest of my time -- the rest of his time will be on me, rather, so could he please finish today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Mr. Hannis, the general practice we were following in the Prosecution case was equal time, not equal of anticipated time, but actual time used. So let's see how we get on. And before you start, I take it the lack of activity to my right suggests no one for any of the accused wishes to cross-examine this witness. All right. Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and I will try and do my best to finish before the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you began your testimony yesterday, you told us how you had been the president of Montenegro and you remained in that office until the beginning of 1998; and then in May of 1998, you became the prime minister of Yugoslavia. During that interim, hadn't you actually stood for a further term as president of Montenegro and been defeated in that election by Mr. Djukanovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the term of office was supposed to expire in January, and the election was called in October. As for the run-off of the presidential elections, I took part in that as the candidate who had the largest number of votes during the first round of voting and Mr. Djukanovic. After many controversies, Mr. Djukanovic won the election, and he became president of the Republic of Montenegro. And that was the reason why there were internal political changes in Montenegro itself, and, therefore, the parliamentary majority was changed. I talked about that when I was -- when I spoke about that being the main cause of the changes at federal level.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. It's fair to say that you and Mr. Djukanovic were political rivals, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This often happens in politics. For years we were allies and inseparable friends. This lasted for almost eight years, and then we had a political clash, not a clash at a personal level.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 13800 from the transcript, you mentioned that the federal government, before you came on board, had been headed by Prime Minister Dr. Kontic, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The federal prime minister until then did not react to reality. He lost support in the federal parliament, and he got more support in the republican parliament.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the OTP's microphones please be turned off the witness is speaking. We have great trouble hearing the witness because of the noise from this side. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll try and do that. May I inquire, is it because the printing is going right now; is that the problem?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Probably. We hear something that makes it impossible to hear the witness properly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you proceed, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Bulatovic, what office do you hold now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have not been in politics since 2000. I work in the private sector in the field of education and consulting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your answer about the changes that occurred then, you mentioned that the federal government headed by Dr. Kontic was toppled and that you got a mandate to form a government. What was the event or the events that led to that federal government being toppled?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The major changes that had taken place in the internal political life of Montenegro as a member republic of the Federation, there was this crisis in the ruling party where I was president and Mr. Djukanovic vice-president, resulted in an extraordinary congress of the party. And it is a fact that another lady came to head the party, but the party split in two. A new party was established: The Socialist People's Party of Montenegro that selected me, and the MPs who constituted a majority in the republican parliament opted either for one or the other. That is how this option was constituted in Montenegro. Mr. Djukanovic was at the head in a political sense, but that particular option with only a few seats by way of a majority insisted on working on the independence of Montenegro and cooling off relations with Serbia. That meant going against the grain of the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And may I ask what you meant when you said you "got the mandate to form a government." From whom did you get the mandate? How did that work?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's prescribed by the constitution, and practice shows that it is the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that gives the mandate for establishing a government. After the previous prime minister lost his vote of confidence, then I got the mandate. In accordance with parliamentary practice, I had to consult all political parties in parliament and to see to what degree my personality was acceptable and my programme. It is with pride that I point out that I won a two-thirds majority of all MPs in the parliament, although at first those political parties did not join the federal government. They supported me as a person and my programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But who put your name forward as the proposed candidate to be the prime minister? Would that have been Mr. Milosevic, as president of the Federation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've said that, and I do hope that the interpreters recorded this properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. That may have been my confusion rather than anybody else's. Now, you mentioned, also, that when you came on board the federal government had previously been constituted in terms of the deputy prime ministers, et cetera. You didn't make a lot of changes, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite precise, I claim that I did not change anything, except for that part of the federal government that came from Montenegro. And due to the political situation that I've already described, they did not have an interest in participating in the federal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So Mr. Sainovic had already been a deputy prime minister when you came into your position, and you kept him where he was, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to put it in the most precise possible terms, according to our constitutional system, a government is elected when the prime minister designate and his programme wins support. We had a chancellor-based system then, and I just informed the government about who would actually be on the government. The government could not decide on the persons who would be in the cabinet. The only vote that was taken was in favour of the prime minister or against the prime minister. So to be quite precise, yes, Mr. Sainovic was again appointed prime minister --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Deputy prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Now, at page 13802, Judge Bonomy asked you a question about the security services not having been set up at the federal level at the time you were the prime minister, and you said: "We never managed to bring together all of these services as envisaged by the federal constitution." You're talking about the federal constitution of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the constitution that was in force then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct me if I'm mistaken, but in 1993 there was a federal security service or a federal MUP, correct, in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the federal Ministry of the Interior. In it were over 1.000 staff members, or rather, policemen. These policemen were used exclusively and only to provide security for embassies and residents and other diplomatic buildings in Belgrade and to provide security for federal buildings, federal government buildings. When talking about the security service, I'm not talking about the police. I am talking about intelligence and security services that are -- that are an integral part of all police forces. So to be precise, the federal MUP did exist, but the federal security service did not exist. And it was the poorest-equipped and least-paid part of our MUP. Actually, they were guards of diplomatic buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There was a federal Minister of Interior?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and what I said goes for him and that is that he did not fully manage to develop his powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was that Mr. Gracanin?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- oh, yes. Yes, you're right. When the first government was established, it was the former Partizan General Petar Gracanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who succeeded him?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pavle Bulatovic, a minister who came from the Republic of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who later became a Minister of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He later became a minister of defence, and he was replaced by Zoran Sokolovic from the Republic of Serbia. He became the federal Minister of Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But as I recall in addition to the federal MUP performing those services, as you said, of being guards at embassies and that kind of thing, in 1992, in the summer of 1992, I'm aware - and correct me if I'm wrong - that there were police from the federal MUP who were sent to Bosnia to assist in fighting the war on behalf of the Republika Srpska, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as far as I know. That is not correct. The decision to establish the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was made in a political declarative sense on the 27th of April; then, on the basis of that constitution, elections are carried out in the Republic of Serbia and in the Republic of Montenegro, as well as at federal level. You know, as well as I do, that a state does not come into being for a single act of political will. It is a process that requires building. So it's only in 1993 that state organs came into being on the basis of the constitution of 1992 and the elections held late in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you're aware that, in the summer of 1992, Mr. Karadzic had requested assistance in dealing with paramilitaries that were active on the territory in Bosnia and that Mr. Gracanin had sent some federal MUP police to help arrest those paramilitaries, including Red Berets and Yellow Wasps, et cetera. That was a highly publicised event. You're aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. This is the first time I hear of it from you, and I think that the story is way too naive. At the moment when we made a discussion, under great pressure from the international public to withdraw units of the Yugoslav People's Army, we made a declaration stating that not a single member of our army or police did not cross the border of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in an official capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then I take it you haven't read the evidence of Mico Davidovic, who was the top-ranking policeman in the federal MUP at that time, about doing just that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two things: First of all, I don't know what this has to do with the examination of the witness who came to testify about something else. Secondly, and more importantly, if the OTP believes that they do not have enough time for cross-examination, I would like the Trial Chamber to bear in mind what it is that Mr. Hannis has been spending his time on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it goes without saying, Mr. Fila, that we will do the latter. So far as the former point you make is concerned, then it appears entirely relevant to a number of issues that arise here, both in relation to the facts and to the credibility of the witness. So please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, do you need me to repeat that question or can you recall it and answer? You haven't seen the evidence of Mico Davidovic about having --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I haven't. Never crossed my mind. This is a completely different level of thinking, different level of working. At that time I was president of the Republic of Montenegro, and in no way and on the basis of no powers could I go into who was doing what there. So I'm not a good witness for this kind of question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But really, Mr. Bulatovic, you've written a couple of books about events in Yugoslavia during the 1990s, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To be more precise, two books.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I guess the point I was driving at was your answer was it hadn't been able to set up a federal MUP in Yugoslavia, and the point I'm trying to make is: There had been one, but in 1993 Jovica Stanisic and the Serbian MUP actually took physical steps to do away with the federal MUP, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're talking about the affair of taking the premises, the building of the federal MUP, then we can agree on that. At that point, Pavle Bulatovic was Minister of Police. Due to some internal misunderstandings, people came and took up these premises; and to my mind, this is proof of the contrary in terms of what you've been saying. That means that the MUP was so strong that they could take buildings physically without expecting any problems or resistance. From that point onwards, there was this strong degradation of the federal MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 29, line 16, the witness was talking about the MUP of Serbia, and here we do not see which MUP he was talking about. Quite simply, it's not in the transcript right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I was going to follow-up on that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, when you say that people came and took up these premises of the federal MUP, you mean people from the Serbian MUP came and took over the premises, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in effect, after that, that meant in terms of what you talked about security services and intelligence and those secret clandestine kinds of things that a security service does, that meant in effect that in Yugoslavia the Republic of Serbia MUP was the one that was doing basically all that work?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly what the MUP was doing. I can only assume what it was that they were doing, but all the main technical resources that belonged to the federal MUP until then came under their jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me move on to another topic. You mentioned in an answer to Mr. Fila yesterday about what you saw as the heart of the problem regarding the conflict of Kosovo, and you said: "There are many facts and many statements and a lot of evidence showing that what was underlying was the wish to create a united state of Albanians in this area. Some people call it a greater Albania." Wasn't the heart of the problem in Kosovo the loss of autonomy that the province previously had and the desire of Kosovo to be independent?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I still stand by my own words. I tried last time but His Honour stopped me. I tried to explain that this was not a problem that cropped up just now or in a certain period of time only. If you allow me to explain, as a young assistant teacher at university, I was quite passionate --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you. I'm not asking -- you've answered my question. Thank you. Were you familiar with a document called the "Kacanik Constitution"?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you keep taking me back to the past in terms of what suits you, but it's hard for me to work that way. I know it is some kind of an illegal document proclaiming the independence of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You've mentioned greater Albania, and you've also heard of the terms of "greater Croatia" and "greater Serbia"?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. But as far as a greater Albania is concerned, I looked at many web sites and many political programmes that speak with pride of this rather than conceal it in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And aren't there web sites that proclaim with pride greater Serbia and greater Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If that is going to make our joint conscience feel better, then yes. But we are not talking about only individual factors here, we are talking here about something that neighbouring countries have to deal with seriously, including Greece and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, in this case, so far, we've seen a lot of documents and heard a lot of evidence about the attempts to negotiate with the Kosovo Albanians and the role that certain international groups and individuals played in those efforts to have negotiations. And it seems to me that the bulk of that evidence has shown that the heart of the problem was Serbia wanted to may not their territorial integrity, which they saw as keeping Kosovo within Serbia, and the Kosovo Albanians, which constituted, I think you agree, a substantial majority of the population in Kosovo, wanted an independent Kosovo. Wasn't that the heart of the problem, that fundamental disagreement?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the starting positions, but I still don't understand what your question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Rugova advocate for a greater Albania?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He advocated something that implied the first step in achieving that goal, which is an independent Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear him advocate for a greater Albania, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me move on to another topic. Mr. Fila was asking you yesterday, at page 13807, about how arming was financed in Kosovo and Metohija, and his question was at line 10: "I wanted to ask you how arming was financed in Kosovo and Metohija." Your answer beginning at line 12 was: "According to all the knowledge I had as president of Montenegro and later as prime minister of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, a significant share of the financing was accounted for by the Albanian mafia." Now, I guess you understood Mr. Fila's question to be about arming of Albanians in Kosovo; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now looking at the transcript and listening to you, there may have been an error. I understood Mr. Fila's question not to refer to the regular army but to where weapons arrived for the terrorist groups that were being established in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And under all the circumstances, I don't think that's -- I don't think that's something to criticise you for. I can see how you would understand it that way, but my question is: What about arming of the non-Albanian civilians in Kosovo? I think you've mentioned a number yesterday of how many non-Albanians you thought were living in Kosovo in 1998. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only number I know I mentioned explicitly was the members of the Turkish ethnic minority. There were 40.000 of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, in fairness to you, sir, I may be getting confused with something Professor Markovic might have said. I seem to recall a figure of 600.000 being mentioned; and if that's his number, would you agree or disagree or do you know?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to add to the confusion, I really am not sure what you're asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm asking if you're aware of the approximate number of non-Kosovar Albanians who were living in Kosovo in 1998; if you don't, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really didn't deal with this, but I think there were about 300.000 non-Albanians because I know thousands of them left Kosovo after the arrival of the UN peacekeeping forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that's in, you mean, in June 1999?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But for those non-Albanians who were living in Kosovo in 1998, you're aware that substantial numbers of them were provided --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see -- I'm sorry. I see Mr. Petrovic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's probably something to do with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Page 33, line 19, the witness said that 250.000 non-Albanians left Kosovo out of 300.000. It says here just "thousands." I think this is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So I was starting to ask you: Are you aware that substantial numbers of those non-Albanians living in Kosovo in 1998 were provided weapons by the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned, at page 13807, yesterday, when talking about your allegation that the Albanian mafia was financing a substantial portion of the money going to arm Albanians in Kosovo, you said: "I had many opportunities to talk to representatives to foreign countries, especially the European mission, or rather, ambassadors of EU countries. I understood that they had similar information and they shared the same kind of concern." Can you name some of those ambassadors who had similar information and shared their concern with you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, almost all those I talked to. What sticks in my mind is a meeting I had in 1996 with Mr. Klaus Kinkel, the then Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Federal Republic of Germany. He told me that it was his job to solve the issue of 100.000 political asylum seekers who had arrived in his country from Albania. They were putting a strain on the welfare system and they were involved in crime. As Mr. Kinkel told me, they were saying as the reason or their asylum seeking the problem of Milosevic and the repression of his regime and there was nowhere to send them back. So Mr. Kinkel kindly explained that they wanted to create an independent Kosovo where they could repatriate those elements that were causing so many problems. The British diplomats especially spoke of life in London becoming almost impossible thanks to the activities of the Albanian mafia, and the same situation obtained in Rome and Paris.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you name those diplomats who told you that from Britain, Paris, Rome?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The representative of Italy was Riccardo Sessa. He was the ambassador at the time, but I can't remember the others. I'm referring to the accredited diplomatic representatives to the FRY in the period from 1995 to 1998. Ivor Roberts was the ambassador of Great Britain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kinkel didn't claim to you that all 100.000 of those asylum seekers were criminals, did he?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, he didn't. That's common sense, but he described the problem as it was seen by him and his government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila asked you, at page 13808: "Did our government warn against this, and did our government ask for this to be stopped," meaning the funding of weapons by the Albanian mafia. Your answer: "We did that systematically, but the this was never reflected publicly." What do you mean you did that systematically? What did your government do in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We tried to be a responsible government for fulfilling its international obligations. Yesterday, when asked by Mr. Toma Fila, I said that we sent regular reports to the UN Committee for the Prevention of Torture in January 1999 in various associations, through Interpol, through the coordination we had. We were duty-bound to provide neighbouring countries and international organisations with our information and ask for assistance, and this is done by every police force in the world under normal circumstances. If you have someone engaged in a criminal activity, the various police forces communicate with one another, and their collective information is used by politicians who try to solve the problem at the level of Interpol, at the level of Europe, because this was such a serious problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where would those records be archived in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. But I think while our country was a member of Interpol, there was very good cooperation because many of the drug routes went through the Balkans, and many criminal groups were exposed and discovered in this area --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, I know you want to get the out of here today, and I'm going to try to do that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment. In 1998, was Albania a part of Interpol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was, if they had recovered from the breakdown in 1977 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You say that: "In private, everyone agreed to us; but in public, they always said, 'No, no, that's not the case. You're just using this as a pretext in order for you to carry out some kind of strange policy of your own in Kosovo and Metohija.'" You say everyone agreed with you. Certainly not everyone agreed with you, did they?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. Most of them did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And when you said "strange policy," what are you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what the international media and some countries accusing the FRY, how they interpreted our behaviour, my expression was not very precise and I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's all right. And some of those that did not agree with you, they were talking about what they perceived as the policy in anti-terrorist operations to use the army and the MUP in ways that they saw as involving disproportionate use of force and indiscriminate use of force against civilians, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think the context was quite different. Those who privately agreed with us, but were unable to support us publicly, were not moved by those motives but by motives of their understanding of reality. Nobody wanted to support a small country while exposing themselves to the risk of being misunderstood or seen as an enemy by the biggest and most powerful country. It is my deep conviction that if the American administration thinks you are guilty, nobody is going to stand up for you or defend you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Bulatovic, you answered my question with your first word "no," and then you went on for seven lines. If we're going to finish you today, I need you to try to give me short answers when I ask you questions that call for short answers. Okay. All right. At page --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise, but your question was whether people evaluated us from the standpoint of the degree of activity of the anti-terrorist actions in Kosovo and Metohija, and I said: No, that was not what they were thinking about or talking about. They were motivated by something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question I asked was whether my proposition was correct or not, and you said no. That's an answer. You can stop there. Is that all right? Can we do that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can barely understand it, but it's up to you. You are examining me, but I can say yes or no. However, the truth that I am duty-bound to express here will then remain unsaid.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You've written a book. Do you want to put your book in to tell the truth? Mr. Bulatovic, the Judges here can sort out the truth. Your lawyer will get another chance to ask you questions when I'm done. This process will go faster if I ask you a question which can be answered yes or no or I don't know, I would request that you give me one of those answers and then we can go faster. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I saw you nod your head, but we need an audible answer for the record.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if speed is the main aim.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm trying to accommodate you, sir. I understand you want to get out of here today. You still haven't answered my question yes or no. Is that all right if we proceed that way?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All right. I'll say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 13813, yesterday, you were talking about the difficult situation; and at line 10, you said: "We knew that an armed rebellion cannot be stopped by military or other means alone." This one - I'm not asking for a yes or no answer - can you explain a little for us what you mean by: "It cannot be stopped by military or other means alone." What were the other means you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a government and a politician advocating that force should not be force, that it should be used to the least extent possible; military and other means, military, police, judicial, and so on, repressive means. However, what is insisted on here is dialogue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Does that mean then an armed rebellion can be stopped by a combination of dialogue and military means?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And you would agree with me, wouldn't you, that the international concerns about crimes and alleged atrocities happening did have some basis in fact, that there were some crimes and atrocities that were occurring in Kosovo. You agreed -- you said that yourself yesterday, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're putting very complicated questions to me. Could you please simplify them so that I can accommodate your wish. My answer is: Yes. Unfortunately, there were crimes and atrocities committed against the Albanian situation also. No one can be proud of that, and we took measures to punish the perpetrators. I'm deeply convinced, with all due respect to all innocent civilian victims, that these were deranged or criminal groups, but it was not a planned joint criminal enterprise or any other kind of enterprise. That is what gives me the strength to sit here and face these facts. What we wanted to do was to have a political solution created and to make it possible under stable conditions that all those who committed crimes - and there were very serious crimes committed - to be tried and punished. As the president of -- or the prime minister of Montenegro, I'm proud of the fact that the first civilian court, the Regular Court of Montenegro, in 1993 was the first in the former FRY to sentence three Montenegrins for crimes committed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Three Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and I'm proud of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You don't have any specific knowledge of or figures concerning the number of Serb policemen or VJ soldiers who were investigated or prosecuted for crimes that occurred in Kosovo and Metohija between June 1998 and June 1999, do you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise for interrupting. I apologise to Mr. Hannis. In the previous response, on page 40, in connection with the first case, Mr. Bulatovic said that the victims were Muslims and that three Serbs were convicted. It is not evident here in the transcript. I think it's important to clarify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that these records exist, I know that the records are precise, and I know that they are very great which is of deep concern. Our government proposed to the Federal Assembly to amend the Law on War Crimes committed on Kosovo and Metohija, and we specified that the act of failure to report a crime is also a crime. These crimes are a stain on anybody's face. When in accordance with Resolution 1244 we left Kosovo and Metohija, my government tried through the Ministry of Justice to establish contact with the UNMIK police and NATO to conduct the necessary investigations. We could suppose or receive statements that a group or an individual had committed a war crime, but we had to have a communication with the Kosovo civilian and military mission in order to conduct an investigation. Unfortunately, because of the general political milieu, there were no responses to our inquiries and our letters, so we were unable to complete the job. I would have been much happier had we ourselves managed to punished perpetrators and then you would have less to do here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Some days that would be greatly appreciated, Mr. Bulatovic. You mentioned that your government proposed to the Federal Assembly to amend the Law on War Crimes. Did that proposal get accepted? Did the Assembly pass that law?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We tabled this in the Assembly, but unfortunately the general circumstances were such that we were unable to implement this commitment of ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned, in answering my previous question about whether there were records about these investigations and prosecutions, you said: "I know that these records exist, I know that the records are precise, and I know that they are very great which is of deep concern." How do you know the records are precise? I guess, when you say "precise," do you mean that they're detailed?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that at the beginning of the combat operations, the chains of command of both the army and the police were used to explain precisely how civilians were to be treated. I heard many times from the Minister of Defence Ojdanic and also from the Chief of the General Staff how one should act in those circumstances, but we also heard that, unfortunately, on the ground among the armed men crimes were taking place, and that using the chain of command and the prescribed mechanisms they were acting to bring these men to justice. That was not my job. My job was only to create the general political conditions and to advocate politically that this job be completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your answer, it was translated as the Minister of Defence Ojdanic and also from the Chief of the General Staff. I think -- I understand at the time that General Ojdanic was the Chief of the General Staff. And who was the Minister of Defence at that time, or are you talking about after the war when you were doing this and Ojdanic has now become Minister of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ojdanic became Minister of Defence as of February 2000, so we had a whole year to complete these tasks, and I know great efforts were invested.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the Chief of the General Staff at that time then was? Was that General Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, wait a little. General Perisic was the Chief of the General Staff until November 1998, and then he was replaced by Mr. Ojdanic. And after Mr. Ojdanic was chosen because the then-Minister of Defence died tragically, General Ojdanic became the Minister of Defence and General Pavkovic became Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, I'm still not sure I got the answer to my question about when you say these records were precise, do you mean that the records that exist about investigations and prosecutions of Serb VJ and MUP perpetrators of crimes against civilians in Kosovo? When you say those records are precise, do you mean they have a lot of details about them? Is that what you mean by "precise"?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I received such assurances that crimes had happened, that investigations were underway, and that charges were being brought. I'm not a lawyer, but I know that dealing with one murder produces a vast quantity of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But you yourself, as you say, you're not a lawyer, and you certainly didn't have the time or the opportunity to review that documentation to see whether it was -- well, whether it was accurate for one thing, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, I received assurances from the persons in charge that everything was being in compliance with the law, and I felt that what they were telling me was the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you name who some of those persons were who were in charge in giving you these assurances?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those were people leading the army and the Ministry of Defence, the people I've just mentioned: General Perisic, Ojdanic, Pavkovic. I know that they too in every way condemned any dishonourable behaviour on the part of the soldiers, and they were working hard to earn again the reputation on behalf of the institutions which they led.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move on to another topic, Mr. Bulatovic. Mr. Fila was asking you about the international verification missions that came to Kosovo in 1998. First, I guess, there was the KDOM, and then there was the OSCE-KVM, Kosovo Verification Mission. And you talked about some of the difficulties that presented for Yugoslavia. You said: "In order to communicate with them effectively," and this is at page 13817, line 10, "we simply moved a large number of our facilities and potential over to Kosovo and placed this at their disposal." Exactly what did you mean there about "facilities and potential" that you moved over to Kosovo? It sounded like you were talking about some sort of material things that you sent to Kosovo to assist the OSCE mission. Are you talking about supplies, furniture? What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one thing you must know is that even prior to the NATO air-strikes, Kosovo as a whole was exceptionally poor and underdeveloped. The OSCE monitoring mission was out to verify the situation in each and every part of the province. That was precisely what I meant: The necessary logistics - this is something you mentioned in your own question - the necessary conditions for the Kosovo Verification Mission to be able to stay in the area and continue to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, maybe it's a matter of translation and I misunderstood, but didn't the OSCE mission -- I mean, didn't they basically pay their own way. They had their own vehicles and their own equipment, and they rented their own office space and lodging, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
