utterances.text: You are fortunate not to understand how poor the area is. Money is no use. You can have all the money you like, but you have no office to rent. You have all the money you like, but there are no cars to rent. I don't really think this is a substantial issue; but if, for example, you have this village and no grocer in the entire village, you can have all the money you like but what are you to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, my question is: Didn't OSCE take care of those own things -- those things for themselves? They had their vehicles and they made their own arrangements for where they would stay, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry there appears to be a misunderstanding. Yes, money, but money is no help at all. If you don't have petrol station, where will you get petrol for your vehicle? I don't think this is a substantial issue. I don't think it's worth our time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I appreciate your opinion, sir, but you'll have to let me decide where I go. And right now I'd like to go and take a break if that's agreeable with the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have to have a break at this stage, Mr. Bulatovic. That will last half an hour. Would you please go with the usher, who will show you where to wait, and we'll resume at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm informed that equivalent time with Mr. Fila will take me to just about the end of this session. I anticipate on where I am and how I'm going. It may take a little longer. I don't know if you will be willing to grant me the time, but I wanted to alert you to the possibility that I may ask for it at the end of the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Fila on his feet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm willing to grant all of my remaining time to Mr. Hannis to be used for cross-examination. The only thing I can't grant him is time which the Trial Chamber rules upon which is not my own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, many Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And thank Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, yesterday, Mr. Fila was asking you about what you did in connection with dealing with the situation in Kosovo; and at page 13817, line 15 he asked you: "Did you take a decision to send anyone down there?" And you said: "Yes. If you mean specifically, we took a decision to send a qualified mission there; many diplomats, assistants, people who were good at communicating. I decided they should be headed by the person normally in charge of foreign affairs in Yugoslavia, Deputy Prime Minister Nikola Sainovic." Wasn't there already a Minister of Foreign Affairs for Yugoslavia with a full staff of his own?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a minister, but most of minister's business was about communicating with the staff that was in the country only to a very small degree. My decision - and I still believe so - was a very logical one. Mr. Sainovic was a person with great political skills and knowledge, certainly sufficient to do this kind of work. Mr. Zivanovic had the same sort of skill and knowledge; however, I judged at the time that it would be more useful for us to keep him in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. So are you saying it was your personal decision to send Mr. Sainovic instead of having somebody from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs deal with it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was my personal decision. I still believe it to have been a logical and consistent one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you consult with your cabinet before reaching that decision, or did you do that on your own?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Of course, I did. Of course, I bore in mind all the political realities. Whoever wants to get into politics at a serious level must bear in mind all the realities, but also one's own personal responsibility which is precisely what I'm now speaking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And one of the political realities of that time and place was that Slobodan Milosevic was a person that you had to consider in making all kinds of important decisions at that level, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, that goes without saying. Mr. Milosevic under the constitution was the president of that country; besides, he was the leader of one of the most important political parties represented both in the parliament and in the cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recall when it was you made that decision to send Mr. Sainovic to Kosovo to be the one dealing with those matters?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said yesterday, early June 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you had only been on the job a few weeks at that time, correct? You started I think 20th of May, 1998?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But given the overall political background that I had, it wasn't difficulty for me to come to grips with that particular job. I had a lot of experience with problems like the one I was facing now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And did you have -- well, when did you first meet Mr. Sainovic? Did you have a long-standing acquaintance with him before this?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure how you would define the word "acquaintance." We had been working together for years, and I was also familiar with Mr. Sainovic's involvement in the Socialist Party of Serbia, of which he was a prominent member. I also believed him to have been a highly successful prime minister of the Republic of Serbia. I had followed his work closely for years and had nothing but great appreciation for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You consulted with Mr. Milosevic before taking this decision, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember specifically whether I consulted with him about this particular issue. As I said, the decision was mine. How I reached that decision was a matter of my job which was a political one. I think Mr. Milosevic would have agreed because he himself had a great deal of respect and appreciation for Mr. Sainovic's work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you telling us now you don't remember whether he agreed or whether you consulted with him?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I didn't remember specifically the day, the time, or the meeting, but, yes, I can tell you with certitude that Mr. Milosevic agreed with that particular move.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So I understand that to mean then that it was your idea and Mr. Milosevic agreed with your proposal to send Mr. Sainovic. That's what you're saying, yes?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what I'm saying. It was about my powers. It was about my decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go to Exhibit P289 -- Let me check the honour, Your Honour. It's one of Mr. Bulatovic's books. I believe it's 2895.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you see that on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could just put up the first page, and I'll ask Mr. Bulatovic if he recognises that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And that's you on the cover and that's your book. What was the name of this one?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Rules of Silence."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: "The Rules of Silence." Yes. Okay. When did you write this?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly in 2003 and in 2004. It eventually came out in February 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I want to show you -- I want to read a couple of excerpts from the book pertaining to this matter. In the B/C/S, it's at page number 2 -- we begin at page 282 of the B/C/S version; and in English, we only have the excerpts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, actually, if the usher can help me, I'll hand a hard copy of that section to Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I've highlighted the part I'm going to read from, so you can follow where I am and correct me if there's any error in the translation. "The Federal Government, which I headed, was elected on 20 May 1998. Its personnel make-up, compared to the previous one, did not suffer major alterations." Then the beginning of the next paragraph: "Slobodan Milosevic had only two specific demands on me concerning personnel. The first one was to, again, appoint Mihalj Kertes, the Director of the Federal Customs Administration." And I'm going to skip over to the next page in the English, and it's under the heading: "Kosovo." "Milosevic's second request was to charge Nikola Sainovic, deputy prime minister, with running political activities related allegations concerning to Kosovo and Metohija." Down to the next paragraph: "When he demanded that from me, he said he wanted to spare me." I'm going down three lines: "He got to like me like his junior brother or his son. He knew that all those who were in the chain of political, military, and police command for Kosovo and Metohija (starting with him and further on) will be indicted by the Hague Tribunal. He will not be able to avoid his destiny, but he did not want me to experience the same. I was 15 years his junior. He was concluding a sort of confession of his, and I should have the right to preserve my freedom." The second sentence in the next paragraph: "I knew he was right." Now, does that refresh your recollection, Mr. Bulatovic, about whose idea it was, yours or Mr. Milosevic's, that Mr. Sainovic should be the one to deal with matters relating to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you read is an appropriately selected quote. I understand the lesson inherent in this. You write books to prove the truth, but I'm still adamant about what I said before. It was a request that I could either accept or refuse. The focus here is on Mr. Kertes, and that's how this whole thing begins. The reason being there were diametrically opposed positions between Mr. Milosevic and myself in terms of his nomination, but that went years back. I accepted one of the proposals, and the other was something that went without saying. If you ask me about the continuation of this or perhaps you will ban me from commenting on that. I believe that these words are truthful and well chosen. I simply convey here what Mr. Milosevic told me at the time. It wasn't difficult to draw the inference in view of the overall international situation, that all those who were to head this struggle against terrorism would eventually be indicted by this Tribunal or at least that was our idea of how things would go at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But the point I'm interested in at this moment is whether that version is correct or what you testified to earlier is correct. Was it Mr. Milosevic's idea that you agreed with or was it your idea that he agreed with? It's one of those two.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my decision, a decision that I took, having previously agreed with his idea and proposal in order to ensure that there was some sort of continuity. Even before I started heading the government, Mr. Sainovic had been involved in international and foreign affairs. Kosovo and Metohija now became the most burning political issue in the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So then I take it by your answer, which is, "It was my decision, a decision that I took," then what you said in your book is not true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hannis, that's not the answer he gave. He said it was his decision, and undoubtedly legally that was the case, but he then said: "Having previously agreed with his idea and proposal in order to ensure that was a sort of continuity." And I understood him to be saying it was Milosevic's idea with which he agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're right, Your Honour. He used the word "decision." My question is: Whose idea was it first? And he didn't answer that question so I need to re-ask it, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you not think the second sentence answers that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, it does, Your Honour, but I think it leaves an inconsistency between how it's portrayed in the book and he said here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is undoubtedly an inconsistency, but the witness has not sought to retract anything he said in the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, and he said he wrote the book to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mihajlovic [sic], did you come here to tell the truth -- I'm sorry, Mr. Bulatovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I took an oath to do just that, and I abide by that oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to page 13820. Mr. Fila, at line 4, asked you: "What exactly was Sainovic doing in Kosovo, and we're looking at June, the summer of 1998 after you sent him there?" Your answer was: "We had certain contacts. We had communication during our cooperation; and it was my understanding that while he was in Kosovo and Metohija, he advocated the same political positions and pursued the same diplomatic activities that we as the federal government were pursuing, too." What did you mean by the term "certain contacts"? How often were you in communication with him about what he was doing in Kosovo in the last half of 1998, from June 1998 until the end of the year?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We communicated to the extent that we both deemed necessary. When we didn't do this at regular government meetings, then we were always in a position to establish some sort of direct contact with. Mr. Sainovic as well as any other member of my cabinet had a broad remit. Their task was to implement certain policies, and their own skills and the degree to which they were accepted by certain communities spoke for themselves. I really appreciated their skills, but I don't think there's a single government in the world where the prime minister meets each and every one of his ministers on a daily basis just to check their agendas and their travel schedules.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How often, generally speaking, did the government have regular sessions from June 1998 to March of 1999? Did it meet twice a week, once a week? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, June 1998 to March 1999, as a rule, we would have a formal session on Thursdays. Tuesdays were for the committees. Every time there was a government meeting so much paperwork was required that you practically needed to cart it into the room where the meeting was being held.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And those committee meetings on Tuesdays, did you attend those regularly or how did that work?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As a rule, the prime minister does not attend any meetings of the committees and other working bodies. The president embodies the institution. He's there to receive proposals once a week. Between all of this, he's far too busy with his other work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So, roughly speaking, you would see Mr. Sainovic at least once a week on Thursdays at those formal meetings; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as a matter of principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Outside those once-a-week Thursday meetings, did you have any sort of regular reporting from Mr. Sainovic? Did he furnish you any written reports, or did he call in once or twice a week from Kosovo to tell you what was happening down there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the task of establishing the verification mission based on the agreement between Mr. Geremek and Zivadin Jovanovic implied lots of correspondence and exchange of letters. There was a spot on my own table that marked the point of confluence of all these reports coming in from the various bodies and agencies. I spoke to Mr. Sainovic even outside our formal meetings whenever there was a need to discuss something in relation to Kosovo or anything else for that matter. He was a person who made contact with the international community. He would go to Vienna, for example. He at one point had a state visit to the Nordic countries, if I remember correctly. There was a lot to do with Kosovo, but not exclusively. He was generally working on asserting our positions and bringing our message to those countries that were willing and prepared to hear us out at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. What was the relationship between you as a prime minister and deputy prime ministers? Do -- did they work directly for you? Did you have the power to remove them? How was that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally and legally speaking, due to my chancellor-like authority, I did have the power to appoint and remove ministers, but that is no simple task, nor is any other task of that kind for that matter. It really depends on whether you strengthen or weaken the political support you enjoy in parliament by taking decisions like that. Your hands are tied, in a manner of speaking, because your basic job is to ensure that there's still support in parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So I understand that you would have, at least legally and technically, the power to remove ministers. But what about the deputy prime ministers, did that include them?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. According to our own internal rules, this was a decision that I would make on my own; the deputy prime ministers and the ministers as well as their specific remits. I could shift them from one type of work to another area, another sphere of activity. However, it was the real world, the world outside, that we had to contend with as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, I understand. As a practical matter, it may be a very different situation than what it says on paper you can do. Did you give -- during that time between June 1998 and June 1999 when the war ended, did you give Mr. Sainovic any specific instructions about what he should be doing in Kosovo or dealing with Kosovo situation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General policies, general objectives, general aims were something that was well-known. Of course, we exchanged experiences. Sometimes one spoke on the ground to some specific people, and we shared this with each other. We shared our experiences in order to stream-line our efforts in order to achieving our objective in the best possible way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But I'm still not clear. Did you ever give Mr. Sainovic a specific instruction to do a particular task like: "Mr. Sainovic, I want you to go to Pristina tomorrow and meet with Rugova and get him to sign this document." Did you ever give him any type of specific task like that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it had seemed to me personally to be a mission impossible for quite a long time. I really wanted one of our own people authorised for that kind of task to meet with Mr. Rugova. Please try to understand the sort of circumstances under which this was happening. Bombs were falling all over the place. Communications are down. The main thing was to have a political dialogue. Find the most influential people, talk to them, try to win them over, try to establish some sort of cooperation and dialogue. How did he achieve that? I really don't know how, but I think he did a really good job.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, I'm really trying hard to finish as soon as I can, but I still don't think you answered my question. Did you ever give Mr. Sainovic a specific task; and if so, can you give me an example?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry if we're at cross-purposes, but you'll have to explain what you mean when you say a "specific task." Get into your car, go to that particular street, and track down Mr. Rugova. If that's the type of thing you have in mind, then, needless to say, I never gave him any specific tasks like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever give him a specific task of meet with Mr. Rugova?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only repeat my previous answer. Our objective was to find a political partner, the political representatives. I'd never even dreamt of ever reaching anyone as influential as Mr. Rugova, truth to tell, but I don't want you to be angry with me so let me phrase it in these terms. I did not give orders to my associates. That is simply not the type of person that I am, nor do I believe that they would have accepted that sort of practice gladly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. Now, Mr. Fila asked you about - this is at page 13821 from yesterday - line 2: "Was Sainovic informing you about the situation in Kosovo and Metohija and about his own involvement?" Your answer was: "Yes. We communicated officially at cabinet sessions." And then the next question at line 11 was: "In other words, he was informing you about everything you needed to know?" Your answer was: "Yes, that's right." Let me propose this to you: You can only assume that because if Mr. Sainovic is not telling you about certain things, you cannot know what he's not told you and you can't know if the things that he has held back from you are things you need to know. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, would you agree to this line of questioning: What would happen if it would happen? This is pure speculation. The report was that he received sufficient information. Bombs were falling. He cannot tell him: "Now I'm going to go to the third street on the left, and I'm going to ring the bell twice." This is a deputy prime minister. His general task is to find Rugova, and he informs him about that. I don't understand what this is getting at, just to establish that we don't have enough time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe it wasn't the most artfully phrased question, but I'm suggesting to him that he cannot know whether things that were not told to him by Mr. Sainovic were things that he would have needed to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. I think that may be something you can deal well in submissions, especially bearing in mind that the answer to the question was put into his mouth by Mr. Fila and is of little value.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And I would note also I've been talking about the period of June 1998 to June 1999; and for a substantial portion of that period, bombs were not falling. But that's between Mr. Fila and me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, then let me ask you this: Did Mr. Sainovic ever tell you about meetings he attended with the MUP staff in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He mentioned a few times that there were such meetings, as there were a great deal of other meetings. That is precisely the job of a politician out on the ground, because you see a politician is out there for votes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, you were asked a specific question; you gave an answer. Please confine yourself to the question. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall him telling you about a meeting he attended in May 1999 with the MUP staff in Kosovo, during which he relayed a message from the supreme commander, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general terms, I confirm that I know that he attended meetings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, the problem now?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem is in a question where there's -- that's where the problem is. Where is the foundation? How is the foundation laid for putting this question? Give me a quotation. Who said what, and then let him respond to that. If you're the person who's saying that, then what? You're seeking an answer to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm referring to Exhibit P1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The objection is repelled. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In general terms, I was informed that Nikola Sainovic had activities and talks in the Ministry of the Interior as well. As for this particular case right now, I am not aware of it; but if you show me some documents, I can comment upon them within the scope of my own knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Could we pull up Exhibit P1996, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we need to see page 4 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure where the equivalent provision is on the B/C/S version, but I'll try and locate that for you, Mr. Bulatovic. This document, sir, is in evidence in this case, and it's minutes of a meeting of the MUP staff in Kosovo on the 7th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me to comment on this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, not yet. I'm going to try a find a specific paragraph that I want to ask you about. It's page 4, paragraph 3 of the English; and on the B/C/S, I'm trying to find that reference. It's two paragraphs above where Colonel Janicevic speaks. I think it's page 4 of the B/C/S, and it's the second paragraph. Now, Mr. Bulatovic, I'll read from the English, and you can correct me if the Serbian says something different: "In his concluding remarks, the Deputy Prime Minister, Nikola Sainovic, thanked all police members for achieving immense results, while sustaining losses and undergoing great sacrifices, in defending the country and waging an anti-terrorist struggle to establish general security in Kosovo and Metohija. "He noted that a large number of men had demonstrated exemplary conduct. Those who did not prove themselves and whose conduct was poor should be punished and prosecuted," he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I need to go up one more paragraph, and I think we have to go to the preceding page of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it starts with: "The President of the Republic and the Supreme Commander, Slobodan Milosevic, heard the report of the Commander of the 3rd Army and the MUP Police Staff of the Republic of Serbia for Kosovo and Metohija, and the text of a statement was made public, representing a state directive and order issued by the Supreme Commander, Slobodan Milosevic, which should be relayed to all police commanders as a task assigned by the Supreme Command." Do you recall Mr. Sainovic telling you about this being discussed at a meeting of the MUP staff he attended on the 7th of May, 1999, in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Although I really wish to be helpful, I cannot make comments on minutes concerning a meeting that I did not attend. I cannot go into the authenticity of this. I cannot go into all this detail. I'm not a witness who can confirm any of this. I can just say that I knew that the deputy prime minister, among all his other activities, had many such activities, too. Specifically, you will find better witnesses who can interpret what this meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm just -- I understand that. I'm just trying to determine what he told you regarding what he was doing. Did he tell you between June 1998 and June 1999 about Joint Command meetings he attended? And we have evidence in the record suggesting that he attended dozens of such meetings during that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on. Mr. Fila? No, you withdraw. Very well. Please continue to answer the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already presented my position on the Joint Command. I was not aware of its existence, and I still, to this day, do not believe that it existed. None of this evidence that was shown before this court - and I had occasion to see that while preparing for this testimony and for another one - have made me change my views, so I cannot say anything more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, in preparing for your testimony, did you see an exhibit numbered P1468, which is a handwritten document titled: "Minutes of the Meetings of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija in 1998"? It's over a hundred pages long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the sake of the dignity of this Court, when a document is being shown, it should be said that this is a photocopy and that there is no original, that there is no signature, that there is no date, that some pages are missing, and that this is some piece of paper, a private notebook or something like that, where it is written: "Minutes." One should not say that these are minutes. Minutes are a formal thing. Secondly, the witness said that he had never seen this and that he was not aware of any Joint Command. I really do not see how this assists anyone, but let us have things shown properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Everything you've said, Mr. Fila, is a matter of submission in relation to the value of that document itself. The question is simply whether that handwritten document, titled as it is, was seen by the witness. That's all he's being asked, and there's nothing wrong with that question. So please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, I don't think you had a chance to answer that question. Did you ever see such a document? It's a Xeroxed copy of a handwritten document that appear to be "Minutes," formal or informal, "of meetings of the Joint Command of Kosovo and Metohija in 1998."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Fila, I apologise to you. I had assumed we were going to see the handwritten. There is a handwritten version of this, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I assume that was what was coming on the screen, but now that particular point made by Mr. Fila had validity and you have clarified it. It's a quite a different format that you might have expected him to be shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question was just probing the basis for his opinion; and whether or not he's seen that document, could have a bearing. If he still has that opinion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't deny that, Mr. Hannis. It's the description of the document. What he's being shown is not handwritten.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. The original is handwritten --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I appreciate that, but your question was: In preparing for your testimony, did you see an Exhibit numbered P1468, which is a handwritten document? So it's a rather misleading question in the context of giving him a printed version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the cover is typed, but the rest of the document is handwritten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, all he was shown is the cover at this stage, so let's be clear. Yes. Now you can see it, Mr. Bulatovic, and the question is: Were you ever shown this in preparing for your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw this document, but when preparing for giving evidence elsewhere, in the case of the Prosecutor of the ICTY versus Slobodan Milosevic. I cannot attach any importance or attention to this document. It is a very, very unserious way of trying to prove a thesis through this document. I have already said that I never knew of the existence of any kind of Joint Command, and it is being proven through this piece of paper which does not result in my reaction or in any kind of attention on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You haven't read the contents of this document then I take it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then I take it that you're also not aware that this document was received from General Pavkovic by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That fact does not change my previous statement in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the fact that this document reflects Mr. Sainovic attending dozens of meetings of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija would not surprise you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll withdraw the question, Your Honour. Let me move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about there's evidence in this case from Mr. Rugova's testimony in the Milosevic trial and from his personal assistant, Mr. Merovci, that in April of 1999 Mr. Rugova was being held under house arrest. Did Mr. Sainovic tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need for Mr. Sainovic to talk about that. It was a public fact that people were claiming that Mr. Rugova was not alive; then when Mr. Rugova travelled to Rome, I think, as a free citizen, he changed his political position and his statement which is understandable. However, the fact that Mr. Rugova left Pristina, or rather, Belgrade when he expressed a wish to do so is ample proof for me that he had not been arrested or detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And question is: Mr. Sainovic did not tell you about that, correct? He did not tell you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry. Your question was whether Mr. Sainovic told me that Mr. Rugova was under house arrest, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. In mid-January 1999, did Mr. Sainovic tell you about an event in Racak in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, our government met in connection with Racak, and we received all sorts of information. That is a tragic incident, and I think to this day it had not been fully clarified from the point of view of the role of all the protagonists there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did Mr. Sainovic tell you about that, or did you only learn about it when the government met in one of-- I guess was that one of, their Thursday sessions?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am trying to respond to your questions directly, but I have to tell you that I find it very difficult because in a way it seems that we are in an autistic system. The event that everybody talked about and wrote about was the main subject in political activities, in political corridors, and we were -- and of course in the federal government, too. And we were just trying to establish what the truth was in terms of something that was used as a pretext for bombing our country. My answer is: Yes. Sainovic told me about that. Everybody told us about that. We had no other subject to discuss but that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How did you first learn of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember that. You turn on the TV and you see that. You make a telephone call and you hear about that. It was a public fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Related to what Mr. Sainovic was telling you, did he -- did he also in late September or early October 1998 tell you about an alleged massacre of Albanian civilians in Obrinje, I think that's both Donje and Gornje Obrinje. Do you recall him telling you about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I do not recall and I do not remember a single occasion that Mr. Sainovic told me about any kind of massacre of Albanians, because I lived in the belief that no such thing ever happened except for individual crimes and incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then Racak you had learned about from the TV, not from Mr. Sainovic. You learned about it first from the TV; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, of course not, but if you want to torture me. It is hard to reduce a man who is a prime minister to the level of a semi-idiot. Either an associate of his will tell him that or he will read about it. I did -- I had a responsible job. I saw thousands of people and spoke to them; and as I've already said, it doesn't really matter how I first learned about this public fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that Mr. Sainovic was your deputy prime minister with the responsibility for Kosovo. And there is evidence in this case suggesting that, while he may not have been the first government official to become aware of it, he was one of the ones who received the information early. It seemed logical that he would be one of the first ones to formally advise you of it; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is correct, that you had the impression that that's the way it was or that this is a question? Now, you started by asking, or rather, saying that you had the impression that, and so on and so forth. So what is it that I'm supposed to comment upon? Your impression or what was actually the case or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was actually the case?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry that we do not seem to be understanding each other, but the federal government was a serious institution that had its own system for reporting information. There was a special system of telephone lines, and there was also the possibility of having an instantaneous conference of all ministers, regardless of where they were. When a fact occurs and it doesn't come just out of the blue, all the members of the government are informed accordingly to our rules. That is why I find this confusing when you are reducing me to the level of a man who is supposed to ask his closest associate what it is that had happened or to turn on the TV in order to get things organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So who was the first one to inform you about Racak, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, the information and reporting system of the federal government, the messenger service that existed. For me personally, it is nameless. I do not know who the individuals are who work in that service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to late October 1998. I want to show you an exhibit, P2166. I don't know, Mr. Bulatovic, is it easier for you if you have a hard copy of the document? Is that easier than working off the screen because we have to go from page to page? I'll hand you this and you can use whichever is easiest for you. Sir, this is a -- this is an exhibit in evidence. Our number is P2166. And this is described as: The Minutes of the meeting of the Operations Interdepartmental Staff for the suppression of terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija held at the White Palace in Belgrade on 29 October 1998. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I am familiarising myself with it. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Have you seen it before today?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw it when preparing for my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was that the first time you had ever seen it? You didn't see it in 1998 or 1999?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's when I first saw it, which is only logical since it is marked "Defence" and "State Secret." Such documents were not freely distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you'll see in the first paragraph the names of all the people attending this secret meeting. Mr. Sainovic was there. Did he tell you about this meeting in 1998? Did he tell you in 1998 or 1999 about this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume that there were several such minutes and several such meeting, so my answer to your question is: Yes. In principle we were always kept abreast, and we were discussing our policy in Kosovo and Metohija. Among the list of participants, I do not see my own name, so this constitutes a great difficulty for me; that is to say, I find it difficult to interpret these minutes from the point of view of authenticity and the reliability of individual statements made.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, sir, that's a -- authenticity and reliability is an issue for the Judges here, but you will see in the second paragraph, where Mr. Milosevic is opening the session and talking about the agenda, he mentions that General Pavkovic and General Lukic are going to speak, as well as Mr. Minic, whom you know. And it says General Pavkovic is going to present the proposals of the Joint Command. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I would like to be precise. I am not a person who is going to judge whether this is authentic or not. Of course, others have that right. I'm just saying that it's impossible for me to interpret minutes from a meeting that I did not attend and to interpret individual --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All you've been asked is whether you see that there is in this document a reference to the Joint Command. Now, that's a question you can answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do I see that "Joint Command" is mentioned? Please tell me where is this. Where is this paragraph where "Joint Command" is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The second paragraph under the big paragraph listing all the persons attending, near the end of that paragraph, it says: "General Pavkovic would then present the proposals of the Joint Command." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is: Yes, I see that. It's written there, "the proposals of the Joint Command," but to me it still does not mean that there is actually a Joint Command in existence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've said that many times and we've heard that many times, so there's no need to constantly repeat it. But I am concerned about what you say about the authenticity of this and its reliability. I entirely appreciate that you cannot vouch for its authenticity and reliability if you were not involved, but are you saying that there is anything on the face of this document, when you look at the stamps and so on on it, that would indicate that it's not an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It appears to be authentic, but only those who attended the meeting can actually confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's not get bogged down in that issue, and let's concentrate on the terms used in the document. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, I guess, I want to ask you again. Mr. Sainovic is attending this meeting, and we've -- we can see from the contents that the Joint Command is discussed at some length. And it's still your position that you're not aware of the existence of the Joint Command, and I take it also that Mr. Sainovic never told you about the Joint Command. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My position is still that I do not know about the existence and I do not believe in the existence of the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you agree, however, that your deputy prime minister with the responsibility -- who's sent to Kosovo to deal with the situation there, a Joint Command would be something that you would expect him to tell you about? Wouldn't that be something that you would need to know from him?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. It's hypothetical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is hypothetical, Mr. Hannis. Let's prioritize what needs to be asked. I think there's enough material there for us to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me move on. I'm going to come back to Joint Command in a minute, but I want to talk about something else for a moment. At page 13822, Mr. Fila was talking with you about the Supreme Defence Council; and at line 14, you answered him that: "The main strategic decisions were adopted by the Supreme Defence Council, and the implementation of those decisions was envisaged in great detail in the existing Laws on Defence and the Army." What about the use of the MUP, of the police, is that detailed in the Law on Defence and the Army?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Law on Defence and the Law on the Army were laws on the federal level because the Yugoslav army was a federal institution. The Yugoslav Ministry of the Interior acted in provisions which I believe were precise and clear contained in the Law on Interior of the Republic of Serbia. This was a competency at republican level.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Were you aware of a provision in either of these laws you mentioned that called for the subordination of the MUP or the police to the VJ during a state of war for engagement in combat activities? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslav constitution envisages that should a state of war be declared - and, unfortunately, this did happen in Yugoslavia - a legal provision enters into force on the resubordination of all local units on the ground to the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you told us earlier in your testimony that you're not a lawyer, and you're not an expert on the constitution, correct? Regarding your background, did you do your compulsory military service when you were 18?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By your leave, just a correction. I'm not a lawyer; but as an economist and as a person in politics for a long time, who was in politics for a long time, I think I have quite a good understanding of constitutional law because I participated in the drafting of two constitutions: One of the Republic of Montenegro and the other one of the FRY. The answer to your second question is: Yes. I did serve in the former Yugoslav Army, and I completed reserve officers' school when I was 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in 1983 in Sarajevo, and the other part was one year in Dubrovnik in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what year was that in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1983 to 1984.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Fila asked you, at page 13824, about whether you knew if the army could have been used to combat terrorism and secure members of the army, secure roads, without necessarily introducing any one of the so-called irregular states: State of emergency, imminent threat of war, state of war. You said: "We spoke about that to the Supreme Defence Council in can't and November 1998," then you said: "The army was being used in compliance with orders from the federal government down the border belt, and then the army is used to defend itself and no order is required for something like that." You're aware, sir, aren't you, that this was a controversial issue, at least between General Perisic, the Chief of Staff at that time, and Mr. Milosevic. You're aware that was an issue of contention between the two of them in the summer of 1998 and up until the time Perisic was replaced in November?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And your question is: Am I aware of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of it. I even know all the details from that period, and I consider that General Perisic was replaced with good reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we show the witness Exhibit P717, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware that in July of 1998 General Perisic had written a letter to Mr. Milosevic complaining about certain things regarding the army and how it was being used in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I have a copy of this letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm sorry. I don't have a hard copy with me, Mr. Bulatovic. But if we could go to the second page of the B/C/S document, maybe we could start there. Okay. I don't know if you can see that on your screen. Do we need to enlarge it for you a bit?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be grateful if you could. That's enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you see this is dated the 23rd of July, and I would tell you on the last page it appears to be signed by General Perisic. He's complaining about some problems with the army. I think number 1 there, he complains that it's being used outside the institutions of the army. Were you aware that his position was that the use of the army to -- in these anti-terrorist actions outside the border zone of Kosovo, his position was that that was unconstitutional and that it could only occur if there was a declaration of one of the irregular states. Were you aware that was his position?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Fila on his feet. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection, but please give him time to read the letter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've read the first page, but I would be grateful if you could show me the second page as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we do that, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We can show him on e-court, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- I don't have hard copy with me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I remember this letter vividly. I received a copy at the time; and because of this letter, I advocated the replacement of the Chief of the General Staff. He would have been replaced in any other country had he sent a letter with such contents. I'm asking Your Honours to pay attention to page 2, where the Chief of the General Staff comments on decisions of the parliament and the Assembly of a country. From the standpoint of democratic principles and practices, this is inadmissible. The Chief of the General Staff can act within the framework of a democratic system and has to respect the decisions of the parliament and the government. It's not for him to criticise. It's for him to carry out, to implement. If you could please turn back a page or two, I wish to draw your attention to what General Perisic actually wrote to the president of the FRY. He says: "There is a constant tendency to use the VJ outside the institutions of the system." He doesn't say it's actually being used. He's saying that somebody's constantly trying to use it. He says that units are being separated out of the doesn't. He doesn't say what units or where. He speaks about attempts to command the units of the VJ by persons who are not competent to do so; however, this is only an attempt. Fourthly, going over the heads of persons in the chain of command, let's say that can really be a problem. Five, conducting a personnel policy on illegal and unprofessional bases. I don't know what that refers to, but it's not for him, it's for the Supreme Defence Council. And, also, about materiel contributions made outside the law and about expenditure, that would be in his competence, yes. I asked for him to be replaced although I had known him for years and had had a good opinion of him. Because, quite simply, it is not the army that can decide whether a state of emergency should be declared or not, it's not for the army to assess what the state budget should be, so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In item number 3 of his list of things that he was complaining about, that's the one that talks about unauthorised persons attempting to command VJ units. And further on in the letter, where he talks about the specifics of that, one of the persons he mentions is Mr. Sainovic, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to show me where this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we can go to the B/C/S page that has item number 3, I think that might be page 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Hopefully, you'll have it soon, Mr. Bulatovic. Yes. You see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Point 3: "Attempt to exercise command over the VJ," so it's "attempt"; and then B: "Attempts by the civilian part of the staff to command the corps." Evidently, General Perisic does not allow that. The entire spirit and gist of this letter says that he will not allow it. I don't know whether Mr. Minic and the other one tried to do this or not, but it's evident that there is a principle of singleness and unity of command and that Mr. Perisic is standing in the way of such attempts. I don't know whether such attempts actually existed, I doubt it, although it would seem so from his letter. However, Mr. Perisic is simply presenting himself here as a person who is asking a lot more than he has a right to in his position as Chief of the General Staff, especially when it comes to declaring a state of emergency and the size of the state budget.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you would agree with General Perisic that it wouldn't be appropriate for Mr. Sainovic to be commanding VJ units, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, independently of this, I had already said that Mr. Sainovic would not even try that. And even if he did try, the generals, the army, and the police would not allow it. These are people who would not allow such a thing. This letter actually shows that this person wouldn't allow it, and he is actually presenting an ultimatum of sorts to the addressees of the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I agree with all that, but I'm not sure you answered my precise question, which was: Wouldn't you agree with me it would not be appropriate for Mr. Sainovic, as a civilian and not the president of the FRY, to command VJ units?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree it would be inappropriate for the deputy prime minister of the federal government, Nikola Sainovic, to exercise command over the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when did you first see this letter and become aware of its contents?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The moment it was sent. This problem also had to do with my own competencies because funds are mentioned here. This was within the competence of the federal government. And Mr. Perisic had more than once insisted that a state of emergency be declared, and the government and Assembly did not wish to do so and that was their right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was it just the government and the Assembly that didn't want to do so, or wasn't it primarily Mr. Milosevic who didn't want to do so?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody serious wanted to do so. Hypothetically speaking, even if the cabinet had wanted that, it would not have passed through the Assembly. Even had Mr. Milosevic wanted to, the Assembly would not have passed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, now you seem to be speculating, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm saying that based on my experience and the facts I saw. It's not speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Article 4 is talking going around the chain of command. Were you aware of who that might have referred to at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not within my sphere of competence, nor was it something I was interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let's go to your testimony at page 13826 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if you're moving away from that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- I have one question. Yesterday, when you were asked by Mr. Fila about this topic and the use of the army, you confined your answer to saying it was a matter for the government to determine the extent of the border belt, and your evidence seemed to envisage only using the army within the border belt. You'll see in this letter that one of the points being made is about anti-terrorist actions outside the border zone of Kosovo, and that this was unconstitutional. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I do not, because besides these activities, the army was duty-bound to defend itself and its members. Terrorists have military facilities and units as their targets. The army was withdrawing from barracks in order to preserve its human and other potential. It was duty-bound to respond to every attack. That's what the Laws on Defence and the Army of Yugoslavia prescribed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I have a follow-up question to that I guess, Mr. Bulatovic. It seems from the evidence we've had in this case that there was a lot of discussion about expanding the border belt. And if the army could basically defend itself and its members wherever they were - and there was some evidence about, well, they can defend the lines of communication, the roads - if that's the case, then why is it necessary to expand the border belt? Because if you take the view the army can take action anywhere in Kosovo, then what does it matter what size the border belt is? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I have already said that, in relation to similar problems, the Government of Greece issued a decision about an extremely broad border belt. A border belt implies the power of the army to act towards civilians in such a way that they have police authority; in other words, they can stop them, ask for their identity papers, their passports, and bring them in, just like the border police. So the reason for having a border belt is that the army has broader powers so that it can correct the border in depth because of the huge pressure of terrorist groups and armed groups and the Republic of Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The evidence in this case suggests that the army outside the border belt, in June, July, through October of 1998 or at least the end of September 1998, was supporting the MUP in anti-terrorist operations; and in doing so, they were using heavy weapons, including tanks and artillery weapons. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in principle I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And isn't that the very thing that General Perisic was complaining about, that kind of activity outside the border belt without a declared state of emergency?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already given my interpretation of General Perisic's letter here, and my answer to your question is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Mr. Milosevic didn't want to declare a state of emergency because he feared that would give the international community an excuse or a justification to come into Kosovo, correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Fila on his feet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is the second or third time that I'm saying that Mr. Milosevic's constitutional competence was not to declare a state of emergency. If someone has something against Slobodan Milosevic, that's their problem, but don't ascribe to him powers he did not have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, talking about de facto powers as well as de jure powers, I think this witness said earlier that Mr. Milosevic was a man that probably would be consulted on all significant matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not the same thing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've already had an answer, Mr. Hannis, that nobody wanted to declare a state of emergency. Your question is: What was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. What was the reason that Mr. Milosevic didn't want to declare a state of emergency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know the answer to that, Mr. Bulatovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have an answer. I have been saying all along that we were committed to stabilising the political situation in Kosovo and Metohija through political dialogue. Declaring a state of emergency would have sent the message and would have meant that our commitment was to apply force and restrictions in order to deal with the problem. This would have been the message sent first and foremost to the local Albanians. It would have sent them the message that we did not wish dialogue and cooperation. That was the main reason, not how it would be seen in the international community. We wanted to engage in an anti-terrorist struggle, while at the same time offering political dialogue to the leaders of the Albanians in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we take the lunch break now? I'm not finished. I know I'm at the end of my time, but I think I will finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think we need a more detailed commitment than that, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think it will take me 45 minutes, barring any severe obstacles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness obviously has very important evidence to give, Mr. Hannis. It does not appear to us that there has been any significant wasting of time on your part, and therefore we will allow you to continue the cross-examination after lunchtime.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We now have to break for lunch, Mr. Bulatovic. Again, please go with the usher, and we will resume in one hour at 1.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.45 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, I have a few little sort of odds and ends I want to cover with you. I'll skip around and then I'll finish with one or two areas. Exhibit 2D299, we can put it up if you need to see it, but this was an appeal to the world for humanitarian assistance for the federal secretariat for information that you told us about this morning. And in my English copy, I'm reading that it talks about "columns of desperate civilians from Kosovo and Metohija flow in every direction." Were there not any -- were there not civilians fleeing from Vojvodina and Serbia, because they were being bombed as well, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please clarify your question. What I have before me is an entirely different document to the one you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's tab 14 in the binder you have there, if that helps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, tab 14. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes. This is the statement by the federal government which was forwarded to the public through the federal Ministry for Information. It refers precisely to what you have just stated, about your question I mean. Long columns of refugees in Serbia and Vojvodina proper, because bombs were falling all over the territory. So my answer to that would be no. Most of the bombs fell on Kosovo and Metohija, speaking of proportions. There was so much explosives being dropped that military experts were informing me that over 34.000 containers had been used with cluster bombs and over 30.000 missiles containing depleted uranium. It's true that bombs were falling all over Yugoslavia. But with the exception of Kosovo, one couldn't feel the same degree of danger anywhere else, not the sort of danger that would drive people out and make them leave and form these refugee columns which the document speaks about. After all, they really had nowhere else to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I suggest to you an alternate explanation is that there weren't police and VJ personnel driving people out of their homes in Vojvodina and Serbia. Isn't that why there were long columns leaving Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can state with certainty before this Trial Chamber that this was not a state policy, and there was no order like that issued by either the political or the military leadership. If you look at certain acts committed by a certain renegade groups and groups of bandits, it's perhaps easier to explain this; however, this large-scale movement of population occurred during severe air-strikes being carried out by NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I think I asked you earlier today about a report of a massacre of civilians in Obrinje in late September 1998. And is it correct that you were not aware of that? No one told you about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you use such expressions as a "massacre of civilians," this would imply a systematic, large-scale deliberate taking of lives. I never received any information to indicate anything like that. I was not aware of anything like that happening, and I can only say that I hope that it never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's have a look at exhibit from October 5th, 1998. Let me find the number on this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] It's Exhibit Number P1440, 1-4-4-0, and I do have a hard copy I can hand to Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document from General Pavkovic. At the time he was commander of the Pristina Corps in 1998 to the 3rd Army command commander personally. And if you could go to item number 2, which I think I've highlighted on the version you have. And I'll read from it, and you can correct me if the translation is wrong. "Based on combat reports, regular intelligence reports, and based on written reports by all unit commanders of 5 October 1998, the PRK, Pristina Corps Command, does not have information about the alleged massacre against the civilian population in the village of Gornje Obrinje on 26 and 27 September 1998, and also in the period while the plan for fighting terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija from 25 July until 29 September 1998 was being implemented. "Chief of the Pristina Corps command security organ orally informed me about the content of the unchecked information that members of the security service sent to the General Staff of the army's security administration, stating that unidentified members of some MUP units were carrying out combat operations in the village of Gornje Obrinje ..." Yes. "Executed persons taken into custody. This information was not about the massacre of the civilian population as mentioned in the media." So this report seemed to indicate that there was some media coverage about this event. You don't recall reading or seeing or hearing anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So your question is really whether I remember reading or hearing or seeing anything about that in the media. There was a flood of information, and I can't say I remember this particular bit of information. If you want me to comment on the document, I can only say that I find it entirely impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In what way? This is a document from General Pavkovic reporting up to his commander. In what way do you find it impossible?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find it absolutely impossible. I don't know about the military system of reporting. I know what the system is that runs from the General Staff to the state itself or the relationship towards the civilian structures. I know that there are rules governing these relations, too; however, the rules are highly technical and I can hardly be expected to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So you did hear something about this in the media at the time, then, about a massacre of civilians in Obrinje?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't remember specifically. I do, however, know that the media - but the reference here is obviously not to just Yugoslav and Serbian media but world media - addressed the issue of systematic massacres, a large number of crimes, a large number of mass graves. I simply believe that it was the only responsible thing to do for that sort of information to be checked in terms of this chain of command. Again, the media referred to here, in my opinion, are media all over the world and not just the local media in Serbia and Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did Mr. Sainovic ever tell you anything about events in Obrinje, or was your information only coming from the media?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This must be the third time around you're asking me the same question and the third time around I have to say Mr. Sainovic never said that he didn't remember the specific case because of the general flood of information. So my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Maybe there was a translation issue there, Mr. Bulatovic. I don't know if my friends across the way can help me out or if I need to ask another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, it doesn't make English sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was listening to the Serbian and the question was asked three times in the Serbian, but that's the extent to what I can say. The Serbian was translated three times in a row, the same question: Did he receive any information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: By you listening to the Serbian, you're usually able to tell us if there's something wrong with the transcript, and you'll see the answer. The third time around, I have to say Mr. Sainovic never said that he didn't remember the specific case; however, if you're not clear, then we'll get Mr. Hannis to ask again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Fila up.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bulatovic answered the question. He said they were flooded with information. There was a lot being said about that. He doesn't remember the specific event, and Sainovic never told him about it. Maybe we should go back to the audiotapes and listen to it, or perhaps Mr. Hannis should just raise the question again to check.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Your Honours, I see exactly which line you're referring to, and this is not what was said because what follows from this is that it wasn't true that Sainovic never told him, and that's not what the witness said. There is a double negation, suggesting that he didn't tell him, but that's not what the witness said, if my understanding is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, do you want to pursue this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, does Your Honour understand it now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. I don't understand the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, there's some misunderstanding here. My question was: Did Mr. Sainovic ever tell you about that? And I think your answer: No, he didn't tell you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again, my answer is no. In the preceding portion of the transcript, all that's missing is a full stop and that would clarify matters. I complained about you asking me the same question three times in a row; and then after that full stop, you see my answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the problem, Mr. Bulatovic. In English your answer doesn't make any sense, and we don't want to be unfair to you. You say: "This is the third time around I have to say that Mr. Sainovic never told me that he didn't remember the specific case because of the general flooding of information." Well, I think I'm content to note, Mr. Hannis, that the witness was not told anything by Mr. Sainovic about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to show you --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By your leave, Your Honour: [In English] This is the third time around that I have to say that Mr. Sainovic never told me that. I didn't remember the specific case because of the general flooding of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. That clarifies it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. That makes sense. Thank you, Mr. Bulatovic. Next, I want to show you an excerpt from Exhibit P1468. These are the Joint Command meeting notes from 1998. I want to start with page 128 and 129 of the English, and that is page number 115 of the B/C/S. Mr. Bulatovic, I'm waiting for the English, and then I'll start.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I guess we need page 128 of the English. [Prosecution counsel confer].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There you have it, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But we've lost the B/C/S page.
