utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's 115 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's now on my screen. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page in the English, we're talking about the meeting of 26 September 1998. It appears to be 1930 hours, and it says: "Absent Mr. Minic."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then if we can go to the next page in English, I'll continue on with Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was that correct what I read so far as the meeting date and time and Mr. Minic being listed as absent?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm making an enormous effort here. Please don't mind me saying this, but I really don't understand exactly what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's unnecessary, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's no objection to the translation being taken --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- so we can assume it's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The difficulty I think for you, sir, is that you're looking at a copy of a handwritten document, and it may be difficult to read, but I'm going to read what the English has been translated as. General -- it talks about the situation in the field and the security situation, and General Pavkovic says: "The operation in the area of D. Obrinje and G. Obrinje," which I take to be Donje Obrinje and Gornje Obrinje, "is finished. Resistance was strong, but this group was squeezed into a smaller area." Further down it mentions: "BG 15-3 was pulled out to Biric" and "BG 15-1 was pulled out to the barracks." We know from other evidence in this case that that's standard abbreviation for battle group. And then skipping a bit: "BG 549-1 was deployed near Suva Reka." And then General Lukic mentions that: "Donje Obrinje was completed today." Now, Mr. Sainovic is the next one to speak, so it's clear from that that he was at that meeting where Obrinje was discussed, and you told us he never mentioned it to you. I want to ask you a question about Obrinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could bring up -- well, wait a second. Let me maybe do one more thing before we leave that. If we could go to page 134 of the English, and I believe it's 120 in the B/C/S or 121. Actually, I'm sorry. We have to back up one page on the B/C/S to catch the beginning of what I want. Well, I guess we have to back up two pages. I didn't realise that was a blank page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Near the bottom of that page -- or, I'm sorry, near the middle of the page, we see Mr. Radovic speaking, and he makes reference to "Koha Ditore," which we understand was a daily newspaper in the Albanian language in Kosovo, and he mentions the occurrence in Gornje Obrinje. So this was a matter that was being discussed in the Albanian papers as well, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I appreciate your efforts; however, I've already stated before this Trial Chamber that I'm unfamiliar with these documents. This really looks like a crossword puzzle to me, and I understand nothing. How do you expect me to provide a valid interpretation of something that has caused so many problems to the OTP? I find this an insurmountable problem. I really have no idea what exactly this or, for that matter, how I'm expected to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We are receiving an enormous amount of background noise from Mr. Hannis and, therefore, are unable to hear the witness properly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not my intention to disrupt Mr. Hannis's cross-examination, but the etymology of his cross-examination implies this: Did Mr. Sainovic inform Mr. Bulatovic about the massacre in such and such a village. The word "massacre" is not to be found in any of the documents that the OTP are now using. There is talk of an operation, a perfectly normal operation, by the police; therefore, let's not drag matters out any further. If the Prosecutor wants to know whether Mr. Sainovic informed Mr. Bulatovic about some operation, well that's a different matter. That is a perfectly permissible question, but the word "massacre" is not used anywhere. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I wonder in light of what you have said any question would have any value now, Mr. Fila. It's important to be cautious to the extent on which you elaborate in these interventions, which are generally helpful. Mr. Hannis, what is the question you're actually going to ask because I don't think you've asked one yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Hannis, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm on to the next document because I understand his point about he feels unable to comment on this one. I'm going to a Supreme Defence Council meeting that he was present at that relates to this. And I would note the word "terrorist" appears in General Pavkovic's report to the 3rd Army command. That's not my word; I'm taking that from the document, Exhibit 1440.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not "terrorist" that was causing concern; it was the use of the word "massacre."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I meant "massacre," Your Honour. If I said "terrorist," I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bulatovic, I would like to move on to something that may be easier for you to deal with, and this is Exhibit 3D718. These are the -- well, the cover page is the agenda or the notice about the meeting, and then it's the shorthand minutes of the meeting of the Supreme Defence Council on the 4th of October, 1998. I'll hand you a hard copy. And if you want to check it to begin, I think you've told us you did attend that meeting, and you can see who attended the meeting. I want to read a passage from a page that I've put a little red sticky on to help you find, and that's Mr. Djukanovic speaking. Do you find that? I've highlighted his name, I think, where it begins. Mr. Djukanovic is speaking to Mr. Milosevic, and the earlier conversation was about Djukanovic's suggestion that Milosevic make a public statement about what Yugoslavia is willing to do to deal with the situation. He notes that: "The international community mistrusts the statements of certain organs in this state, both on the level of the federal state and on the level of the Republic of Serbia, and their attention is focused on your views," meaning Mr. Milosevic. If you'll go down to the fourth paragraph under his name, Mr. Djukanovic says: "In the talks that I had on Friday," and if we know this meeting was on the 4th of October and in the scheduling it notes that the 4th of October was a Sunday, then Friday would have been the 2nd of October, "in the talks that I had on Friday, and since we'd spoken the day before," approximately the 1st of October, "you had told me something about that Obrinje. "But on the basis of Obrinje, there is complete mistrust that the war activities have been stopped there and there is serious suspicion that Obrinje could re-occur and will re-occur day in and day out." Now, that's what Mr. Djukanovic said at the Supreme Defence Council meeting on the 4th of October, and you were at that meeting. Does that refresh your recollection about whether or not you had heard about Obrinje?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you can see, Mr. Djukanovic participated in this conversation, too, and he talked about Obrinje in very general terms, and he also mentioned the fact that foreigners told him about Obrinje, foreigners with which he had contact. He says on page 29 of the Serbian transcript, he's addressing Slobodan Milosevic, and he says the following: "It's not just the suspicion of those you take to have bad intentions for our state, Mr. President. Hill is also one who is more realistic," and obviously he has Chris Hill, the American ambassador in mind. This individual was trusted as a moderate diplomat I think he was an American ambassador in Macedonia at the time. We met him at the time of the Dayton negotiations. Mr. Djukanovic didn't have any direct information; but as is customary, he relayed his information at the Supreme Defence Council and asked for clarification. Given the text I have before me, I can't see that anyone at that meeting agreed that they should pass over the case in silence. You should read done, but I do remember this meeting. But the conclusion reached at the conclusion was that if the country was attacked it would defend itself, and the president of the Republic of Montenegro, Mr. Djukanovic, also voted in favour of that conclusion; otherwise, it wouldn't have been possible to adopt such a conclusion. The position adopted on page 31 and the conclusion of the meeting, have a look at the bottom of the page, states the following: "Yugoslavia is in favour of peace and is resolved to find a peaceful solution to all problems" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, we're way off the question. Do you recollect there being --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. You're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you recollect there being concern at that meeting that what had happened in Obrinje should not be allowed to re-occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given this document, Your Honours, you can see that what happened in Obrinje is not known, but the American diplomats told Mr. Djukanovic that something had happened. And this document also shows that those issues were on the agenda of the Supreme Defence Council, and state policy wasn't to approve of such incidents and crimes. They launched investigations into such matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you not concerned to know what it was that had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Naturally. Mr. Djukanovic raised the question, and this question had to be dealt with through reports to the relevant command. Perhaps this can be seen in the documents that you are referring to. I don't know how they came to be, though, these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The trouble is you were there and what we're looking for is your recollection, and you don't seem to have any, which is rather strange.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have said, I remember the matter very well. I can even remember the atmosphere that prevailed. Please, if you have sufficient patience, please read through this. This document, this evidence, doesn't say anything about something that happened. It just mentions the fact that one suspects certain things. And Mr. Djukanovic expressed that suspicion, and he was very close to American diplomats at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He was keen that Mr. Milosevic should say something to try to restore international confidence, and, therefore, it was more than a suspicion that he had, surely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that a question or a comment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's a question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that Mr. Djukanovic was a serious politician at the time, and he knew that trust could not be regained so rapidly. But as the meeting evolved, Mr. Djukanovic accepted the proposals made, and the decision was unanimously adopted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At the time Obrinje was a hot topic in Yugoslavia. I think we heard evidence yesterday that -- of communication to Mr. Milutinovic about Obrinje about this time, the first week in October. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall what --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I see --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I don't know to what Mr. Hannis is referring to, the communication to Mr. Milutinovic about Obrinje at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that was Exhibit P2827. I believe Mr. Stamp used it the other day with the last witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that P2827 talks about Gornje Obrinje at all, with all due respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have the document. It says: "Reports in the western media in the Albanian press about an alleged massacre of Albanian civilians by Serbian police in Gornje Obrinje village." It's the first two lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we proceed, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, then I have a question for you regarding Exhibit 2D67. That's tab 2 in the binder you have, I think. This is a document that is described as conclusions of the Federal Assembly on the 5th of October, 1998. My first question I have is: On my English translation, in the upper right-hand corner, it says: "Item number 1, Draft." Is this a draft version of the conclusions, or is this the official, final version that went out?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "draft" in the Serbian language, and this means that it's a document issued by the federal government. It was addressed to the Assembly for a decision to be taken. It was addressed to them as a draft. Once it was adopted by the Assembly, and it was unanimously adopted, then it's given its final form, but the conclusions are the conclusions of the Federal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So this document was drafted by your branch of the government, by the government, and proposed to the National Assembly for them to act upon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On behalf of the federal government, I proposed this to the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who actually wrote this? Was that you or somebody in your office? Do you know who actually wrote the text?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says the government as a whole in the text. As to who actually drafted it, well it's a matter of internal technology. I signed it, and I do agree with everything that is stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this is the -- would this have -- when would this have gone to the Assembly if it's dated the 5th of October? Is that the day it was sent to them?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the preamble, it says that the Federal Assembly took place on the 5th of October. That means it was convened on the 5th of October; and on that same day, after a discussion, these conclusions were conducted. You obviously have a document in front of you that was issued from the government. This is from the government archives. An identical document, but without the term draft and with the signature of the two representatives of the federal council, could be found in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question is much simpler. We know that the sitting was held on the 5th of October. Mr. Hannis would like to know if the government drafted this before the 5th of October; and if so, on what date. Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, probably a few hours earlier or later, perhaps before the 4th of October, on the 4th in the evening, something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know if it was written before or after your Supreme Defence Council meeting where Obrinje was discussed?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had a look at the document a minute ago. I can't retain everything in my head, but if you allow me, the 4th of October at 1600 hours, well, the same time, in fact. At the time we all worked for 12 or 14 hours a day, so we didn't pay attention to the details that you are insisting on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, the reason I ask is if this matter of Obrinje was discussed at the Supreme Defence Council meeting you attended and then you wrote this document after that, I'm curious as to whether you would have made any mention or reference to Obrinje in those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was quite sufficient to have a look at the document that you have presented here and to prove that Mr. Djukanovic only mentioned this and then did not continue to insist on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you told us before that there was a flood of information that you were getting about Obrinje at the time; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said there was a flood of information, but not just about that particular case, about all other cases, and there were -- there was a lot of media speculation, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, when you say "about all other cases," are you talking about all other cases of killings or massacres, or are you talking about everything in general?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about a real media war that was being conducted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila. Hold on Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to object that he shouldn't answer -- Mr. Bulatovic never said that he received information in the way that Mr. Hannis's question implies. Mention was made about a flood of information. He never said that he heard information about Obrinje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, the answer he's just given before this question was: "I said there was a flood of information, but not just about that particular case, about all other cases, and there was media speculation." And Mr. Hannis then asked: "When you say 'about all other cases,' are you talking about all other cases of killings and massacres, or are you talking about everything in general?" Nothing wrong with that. Do you want to add anything to your answer, Mr. Bulatovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I'm saying is that when one goes back to that period of time, I know that my country was exposed to a real media war, and there was so much speculation. There was so many dramatic statements that, given that flood of information, we didn't have the time or the possibility to deal with such media speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bulatovic, does that mean that because there was so much of this international media speculation that you just didn't bother to check out any allegations of mass killings because you couldn't sort out which ones might have any merit?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can do is repeat this. Our position was that force could only be used in accordance with the constitution and with the law, and I do know that the generals provided us with guarantees and stated that they would do all possible to prevent incidents of any kind, executions; or rather, they said that if such incidents did occur the perpetrators would be brought to justice. That's all I know. But as to what CNN and other newspapers published, well fortunately that wasn't true, neither in our case nor in the case of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you saying that anything that CNN or these other newspapers published was not true? Everything they published was false; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, naturally, no, but you have no respect for reality in which we were living. I don't have the right to provide -- to put a counter question to you, but do you think that everything CNN says is true?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you about this one, though. Obrinje was not just another media speculation or an international speculation. This was talked about in your Supreme Defence Council meeting, the two presidents of the republic and Mr. Milosevic. This was reported by one of your generals, General Pavkovic, from the Pristina Corps command to the 3rd Army command, indicating that the perpetrators were from the MUP. Didn't you feel that this was an appropriate one to perhaps do a little further investigation, on the off-chance it might be one of the ones that CNN and the others maybe got right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're taking things out of context. What's the main subject of this discussion? Well, the fact that Mr. Djukanovic turned up and said NATO's going to bomb our country. Obrinje or other events in the area, well, the central theme of the meeting was the risk of the country being bombed, and that is what came to pass. I think that anyone reasonable would pay a lot more attention to such a matter because a small and poor country was faced with a threat from the most powerful military alliance ever formed in the history of mankind. So people sat down and examined the situation, and the conclusion at the meeting was important. The conclusion was they have no reason to attack us. We will try and defend our interests peacefully. But if someone does try and attack us, we will defend ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So can you answer my question or do you just not want to?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have answered your question, with all due respect, and I firmly believe that my answer is the correct one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You'll have to point to me then in your answer where you answered. My question was: Didn't you feel this was an appropriate one, Obrinje, to perhaps do a little further investigation, because the information wasn't just coming from the international media. Did you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir. I have answered the question. I said the subject of the meeting was the serious threat from the NATO alliance, the threat of bombing a country of ten million, and only people who weren't serious would have behaved in the way that your question actually implies. We dealt with matters in the right order of priority.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we show the witness Exhibit P1317. And while we're at it for the record, Your Honour, I should indicate I misspoke earlier when I identified the stenographic notes from the October meeting of the SDC. It is actually Exhibit P2831. 3D718 apparently is -- are the minutes from the meeting. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is 3D718 an exhibit that hasn't actually been admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, apparently it has not. Those are the minutes of the meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. I think there's no English version of them, and that may be why they have not, or it may not be intended to introduce them --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see we have minutes. Yes, we have minutes in English in Exhibit P1575. I think this is one where we had some overlap or duplication with Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For the avoidance of doubt, 3D718 has not been admitted. So let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, this exhibit that you should have before you now --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What I see on my screen is not what I anticipated. Is this -- did I speak incorrectly. I'm looking for P1317, which is a response to a request for assistance from -- received by the OTP from the federal Ministry of Justice from Serbia. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My office, the Prosecutor's office, made a request from the authorities about information pertaining to a Joint Command, and this is the response we received. It indicated: "The Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija was formed on the order by the FRY president in June 1998 without any specific document. The above command operated until October of that year." Now, do you want to take a minutes to read the rest of that, Mr. Bulatovic, before I ask my question?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Could you scroll down, please, so I can see the signature. Is this number, number 12, or is it a signature?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's translated as the initials capital "N" and capital "S," with the full banana, which I think we pronounce as "sh."

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document is dated 2002. I wasn't involved in politics then, and I had no information about who was behind these initials. Do you have a question to put to me, or can I comment on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. I do have a question for you. Does the fact that this is the information we received from the authorities in Serbia about the Joint Command - and it seemed to indicate that there was a Joint Command at least between June and October of 1998 - does that change your prior opinion, where you said you did not believe and you do not believe that a Joint Command existed? Does it change your opinion or not, just yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It just reinforces my claim. This document is not trustworthy because one doesn't know who is behind the initials, and the contents of the document are particularly interesting. How can someone claim that a Joint Command was formed without a specific document being issued. Was it formed or not? Because within the state organs, things are established on the basis of documents and decisions, and then there is a claim according to which a number of unofficial meetings were held. So a body that isn't formed pursuant to some sort of document and has unofficial meetings, well, this doesn't lead me to change my opinion with regard to what I previously stated as far as the issue of a Joint Command is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have a couple more questions for you then to follow-up on that. There is evidence in this case, first of all, in the form of minutes from the meeting of the VJ collegium during 1998 and 1999, in which there are references to the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. If I were to tell you that we do have that evidence, would that change your opinion about whether or not there was a Joint Command in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whenever such a statement is made, I believe the document should be presented. This is the president of the government. He said he had no idea about this. If that was the case, if someone doesn't believe such a thing existed, well, then you should show the relevant documents. But this is a question out of the blue, and I am doubt that that is actually stated. But if that is what is stated, I'd like to see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm -- well, I'm comfortable that that evidence is in the record. I don't intend to show him the document at this point, because I don't think it's a fruitful exercise. I have one more question, and then I'm going to stop. We also have at least one document from General Ojdanic as chief of the -- Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command -- or the Supreme Command Staff during the war, in which he makes suggestions to subordinate units about an order that had been issued by the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would that change your opinion about whether or not a Joint Command existed, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, we don't think that this is going to assist us in any way. Opinion is not what matters here; it's factual evidence. And you've had the answer of the witness repeatedly to the question of the existence of a Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I think you've given him every opportunity to state a different position, if that was the case. If you want to pursue this, you'll need to show him the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We doubt if there's any value in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree, and that was my only purpose. I have no further questions of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I only have a couple of matters to raise. First of all, can we bring up document P1440, page 2 of that document, please, paragraph 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you pay close attention to paragraph 2. Let me remind you. This is a report by General Pavkovic sent to the 3rd Army, the commander, Mr. Samardzic, at the time. If we read this carefully, it seems to follow that based on combat reports, regular operative reports, and based on written reports of commanders of all units, dated the 5th of October, 1998, the Pristina Corps command has no information to indicate that a massacre occurred against the civilian population in the village of Gornje Obrinje. Mr. Bulatovic, would that not constitute proof enough to you - this is the meeting of the Supreme Defence Council on the 4th and this is the 5th - would this not constitute a basis for checking? Mr. Pavkovic addressed the issue, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at these dates, and if you bear in mind the fact that I spoke about the general commitment to check any allegations, then this would be a legitimate inference. I had a private problem because the Prosecutor tried to drag me into an area in which I'm not competent. I am not someone who deals with that sort of thing based on my political or personal affinities, and I focused my efforts on different areas altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, on to the next paragraph. Would that paragraph be consistent with your position, if crimes occurred they were committed by individuals?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my inner-most conviction and that is the general conviction. I know our officers are highly trained. They are honourable people. They went through a lot of training, and they certainly had no chance to develop any racial, religious, or ethnic intolerance in the course of that training.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Let's try to wrap up this document. Is this a document where somebody is checking something that apparently occurred or did not occur?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By looking at this, my impression is they are checking. This is constituting a background check, and this is something I referred to previously during my examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next document, please, P2166.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 3, please, on the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please look at the portion that is underlined.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Further down, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It says: "Pursuant to the decision." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you help me with this, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: "Pursuant to the decision adopted at the 5th Session."

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed: "Pursuant to the decision adopted at the 5th Session of the Supreme Defence Council held on the 9th of June, 1998, the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia, the Law on Defence, and the rules of service of the Army of Yugoslavia, a plan was drafted to suppress terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija envisaging the use of MUP -- Serbian MUP units and the Army of Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So what is that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to make it any clearer than the document we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Based on this, do you infer that the use of those units was constitutional and legal?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is more evidence to support my claim. Everything that was done was done in compliance with the constitution and the laws governing the use of the federal Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. The next thing I would like to bring up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the date of that document? Sorry, the 9th of June. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the following document: 1D139.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's not the 9th of June; it's the 29th of October, 1998. The session was held on the 9th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document that I showed is the 29th of October, 1998, and it's in reference to the session held on the 9th of June, 1998. General Pavkovic -- General Pavkovic is the one who refers to it. Can we, please, show Mr. Bulatovic the following: Article 133 of the Constitution. Article 133. Article 133. Can we zoom in on the Serbian, please, and everyone should have an English copy. Can we please zoom in on Article 133. I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It reads: "The SFRY, as an army, defends four different things: It's sovereignty, territory, independence, and the constitutional order." You've answered some parts of that question already, but I'd like to get more specific than this. You said you were involved in drafting the constitution, the one that we are in the process of quoting, right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does it say anywhere that the Army of Yugoslavia defending its sovereignty, territory, independence, and constitutional order can only ever be used in one of the so-called irregular states?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what follows from this. The constitution is the highest duty of the army. Even if the state leaders decide to give up defending sovereignty, territory, independence, and the constitutional order, the army - at least according to this interpretation - would still be entitled to defend these values. As for specific provisions on how the army was to be used, they are to be found in the Law on Army and the Law on Defence. I'm convinced, because I've discussed this subject many times and I've looked at the provisions many times, that it was not necessary to declare any sort of emergency; or limited emergency was not necessary to restrict human rights throughout the area for the army to be able to perform its function throughout the territory of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What about Article 135?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This article talks about how command is to be exercised over the Army of Yugoslavia. It says that, both in peace and wartime, the president of the republic shall be the commander. The reference here is to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in compliance with decisions taken by the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear or understand Mr. Fila's question. Could he please be asked to repeat the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Therefore, as far as peacetime command is concerned, that's peacetime, right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have the last document brought up, P717. P717.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the document to come up, there was another thing I wanted to ask you about the border belt. Mr. Hannis asked you a thing or two about that, too. I think the depth or the breadth of the border belt was changed by a decision of the federal government at one point. Can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depended on the situation in the border and the lie of the land, and the federal government at the proposal of the army of Yugoslavia takes a decision on the specific breadth of the border belt. It can be 50 or 100 metres from the border, and sometimes the maximum was as much as a 5-kilometre stretch. Because of the lie of the land in the area, one used pack animals. Numerous smugglers used pack animals to smuggle weapons across the border from Albania into Kosovo. Our border patrols normally comprised no more than five to seven members, and there were clashes between armed criminals and our border patrols. These were dangerous clashes and the lives of our border patrol members were at risk. In order to be able to cover certain directions which experience showed were being used by criminals, we had to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the answer has gone way beyond the question at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't understand why these things are just allowed to wander, Mr. Fila. Could we keep some control over the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, but it's probably an error in my legal background. This is the sort of thing controlled by a judge in the system that I come from. In continental law, it's the judge who runs the proceedings. He's in charge. When a judge that judges the merit of the case, then both the defence counsel and the prosecutor must remain silent. It's the same where I come from, but you do have my apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry I'm displaying weakness, and I wish you had drawn that to my attention earlier, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. My apologies. I won't happen again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It was a very general question, and it may be that you were wanting all this answer, in which case you're entitled to get it, but it looked as though we were straying.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I wanted something else altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you remember that the border belt was broadened by 50 [as interpreted] kilometres at one point in time.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely for the reasons that I've tried to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. The reason I'm asking you this --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's an error in the transcript. It should say from 5 to 10 kilometres and not 50 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking you this question is this: A misunderstanding might arise about the use of the army in the border belt and further afield. Talking about those four principles from the constitution, is that something that is restricted to the border belt, or are those the values defended by the army anywhere throughout the territory?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, that is the very purpose of its existence. This is something that the army must do under the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The answer was not recorded. Of course --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, yes, this is something that the army must do throughout the territory, not just within the border belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The right to protect convoys, is this something that applies both in and outside the border belt?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that it applies everywhere and it applies to both the police and the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, P717, can we show page 4 of that document. Could you pull that up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, we see a proposed solution here. But before we get there, as far as I've been able to see, in the previous part of this letter, Mr. Perisic complained about the SFRY government, right, that means you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because we weren't giving him the money he wanted. That was a problem that often occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What about the state of emergency --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think we're on the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. The same page, paragraph 1(A). [In English] English version page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That not the right page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Carry on anyway, Mr. Fila. We'll get there eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now we come to the proposed solution, the proposed solution. The first sentence. Could you please read the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Use the VJ legitimately to defend the border belt, military facilities, and units. Do not use the army for any other assignments or else declare one of the states provided for in the constitution and use the army to its full capacity."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. What I want to know is this: Let's suppose one of the irregular states is declared. To satisfy the OTP, it should be done by President Milosevic, the Serbian government, and the Federal Assembly. What exactly would this imply, use the army to its full capacity in relation to Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only assume what it means, and I shudder to think what it might mean, use the army to its full capacity. That might lead us in an entirely different direction from our political commitments and the political solutions that we advocated.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let's say they blamed us for using disproportionate force in response to terrorist attacks. As you know, the whole world raged against us because of this. Would this be more than the army was actually used?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard this sort of objection being raised by any of my diplomatic partners. The people I talked to, I never heard any talk of disproportionate force. These are serious people; they know what proportion means. Media wrote about this, yes, but there are certain international conventions and norms accepted by our country, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The question is: What sort of use of the army would this be, as opposed to how it was actually used at the time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a hypothetical question. There would have been a full-scale war. They're asking for a state of emergency to be proclaimed, and they're asking for money. My conclusion is they want to go to war.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you infer based on this that General Perisic advocated the use of force to bring an end to this problem?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conclusion that I would draw is General Perisic contributed to his own replacement, but he changed exactly nothing about Yugoslavia's state policies.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the counsel please kindly be asked to make a pause after the witness finishes answering the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please proceed now Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Hypothetically speaking, what if one of the irregular states had been declared? What if the army had been used to its full capacity, as that document states, would that constitute a peacetime policy in relation Kosovo's Albanians, or would this be constituted as an act of someone who is trying to stifle a use of force?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This has nothing to do with a peaceful solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Another hypothetical question, and I'll wrap it up. October 1998, you're a wise and experienced statesman, aren't you? In your opinion, would the response have arrived sooner than it did, which was in March, had we sent an army down there and declared a state of emergency?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is such a hypothetical question. In diplomatic circles, they talked not about a humanitarian disaster in Kosovo, but rather the credibility that Yugoslavia -- that NATO had to preserve in international circles.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. This completes my re-examination. Perhaps the Chamber might like to ask some further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Well, I don't have much to ask except that the Honourable Judge Bonomy had asked you what are you doing now, and you said you were having a different vocation. Do you miss politics?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR BULATOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, under the circumstances within which we were involved in politics and you risked being killed, well, no, I would say that I no longer have any desire to be involved in politics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming here to give it. You are now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll commence with the witness on Monday. This witness will be arriving tomorrow and can only stay for a day. But I think we have deserved a little rest; if not, then take away 20 minutes from my Defence time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it would be cheap at that price, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is one thing we can deal with before we rise, and that is the request by you, Mr. Fila, seeking admission of the written statement of Vasiljevic. In view of the nature of this statement, it could not be admitted without the opportunity for challenge by the Prosecution. It goes to acts and conduct, and it would be wrong I think, even in these unusual circumstances, to admit it without the opportunity. However, we are satisfied that it is an appropriate course of action for the witness to be recalled, and we, therefore, order that you may recall the witness for additional cross-examination on the extract from the diary. The other accused may also apply to the Chamber to conduct further cross-examination of the witness on this limited basis. The motion is thus disposed of accordingly, because the presence of the witness will provide an opportunity for consideration of the admission of the proposed statement referred to by you in the application, but it's a matter for you. You may decide, though, the easiest way is just to ask the witness the necessary questions. We also consider it appropriate not to require Mr. Vasiljevic to return here. So the evidence can be given by video-conference link, and later today a formal written order to that effect will be issued. So you should be able to have him recalled before you conclude the defence case for Mr. Sainovic, and we will make every effort to ensure that you can have the video-conference link facility before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on the 29th of this month a video-conference with Zoran Jelenic has been scheduled. In the meantime, I have spoken to the Prosecution and asked him to contact General Vasiljevic. He's a Prosecution witness, and perhaps an agreement can be reached with him. I really can't make General Vasiljevic come here, but he would probably respond to a Prosecution request. On the 29th, well, it's not a problem. Mr. Mijatovic does not speak at length, and perhaps we could save some time on that day and have General Vasiljevic appear on the same day. If the Prosecution asks him to come on that date, he could then answer all the questions put to him by Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a very helpful suggestion, Mr. Fila, but put yourself in the place of the witness. Would you prefer to respond to a request from Mr. Hannis or a request from you?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I prefer to respond to a request from Mr. Hannis if I was his witness. We'll try and do this together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I assume, Mr. Hannis, that to the extent that Mr. Fila requires your assistance that that will be provided, with a view to having the evidence on the date suggested, which seems sensible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll assist, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, that's got your penalty down to 15 minutes. So we will adjourn now until 9.00 on Monday, and on Monday we will sit to 3.30. And please bear in mind the possibility that on other days next week, we may also do that if we can find a space.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 20th day of August, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.15 p.m.,
